chapters.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
chapters.summary: Introduces simple harmonic motion as a special oscillation where acceleration is proportional to and directed opposite the displacement from a fixed center. Establishes the defining equation a = -ω²x and the restoring force relation F = -kx.

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This text covers the physics of simple harmonic motion, a fundamental type of periodic oscillation. It defines SHM through its characteristic acceleration-displacement relationship and the restoring force directed toward a center of oscillation.

chapters.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
chapters.summary: Introduces simple harmonic motion as a special oscillation where acceleration is proportional to and directed opposite the displacement from a fixed center. Establishes the defining equation a = -ω²x and the restoring force relation F = -kx.

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_1:shm_line>> Why does a swing always come back? Pull it far, it rushes back hard. Pull it a little, it drifts back gently. Something is steering it home. Let's strip away the swing and look at the bare idea. <<SECTION:Simple Harmonic Motion|id=sec-1>> A particle moving back and forth <<TRACE:motion-line>> along one straight line, around a <<FOCUS:center-point>> single fixed point we call the centre of oscillation. <<FOCUS:particle>> Here is the particle, sitting a <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> distance x to the right of the center. We call that distance <<FOCUS:disp-label>> the displacement. Now watch <<FOCUS:accel-arrow>> the one arrow that matters. The particle's acceleration <<FOCUS:accel-arrow+center-point>> always points back toward the center, never away from it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So here is the honest question: is that homeward pull always the same strength, no matter where the particle is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No. The further out the particle sits, <<FOCUS:accel-arrow>> the longer that arrow grows. <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow+accel-arrow>> Double the displacement, and you double the pull back toward the center. <<PAUSE:short>> And the instant the particle crosses to the other side of the center, <<FOCUS:accel-arrow>> the arrow flips and points back the other way. <<UNFOCUS>> It is forever chasing the middle. Let's say that in plain words before any symbols. <<WRITE_TEXT:accel toward center, size grows with displacement|id=text-1>> Acceleration is <<FOCUS:accel-arrow+displacement-arrow>> proportional to how far you are from the center, and it points the opposite way to your displacement. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the center, and points in the opposite direction, back toward the center. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = -\omega^2 x|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:a = minus omega-squared x|id=key-1>> Now the symbols are easy. Acceleration a equals <<FOCUS:accel-label>> minus omega squared times x. <<UNFOCUS>> The minus sign is the word toward; omega squared is just a fixed positive number setting how stiff the pull is. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. The resultant force acting on a particle executing simple harmonic motion is four newtons when it is five centimeters away from the centre of oscillation. We need to find the spring constant. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Resultant force = 4 N at 5 cm from centre. Find the spring constant k.|id=ex-q-1>> Since force equals mass times acceleration, the restoring force is also proportional to displacement and directed back toward the center. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F = -kx|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start from the definition of simple harmonic motion: force equals negative k times x. <<WRITE_STEP:F = -k x|id=ex-step-1-1>> Ignoring the sign, which only tells us the force is restoring, the magnitude of the spring constant k is simply the force divided by the displacement. <<WRITE_STEP:k = F / x|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we substitute the numbers. The force is four newtons and the displacement is five centimeters. But here's the careful part: we must convert centimeters to meters. Five centimeters equals five times ten to the minus two meters. <<WRITE_STEP:k = 4 N / 5 cm = 4 N / (5 × 10^-2 m)|id=ex-step-1-3>> Dividing four by five times ten to the minus two gives eighty. So the spring constant is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_ANSWER:k = 80 N/m|id=ex-ans-1>> Because force equals mass times acceleration, this is the same as saying the force on the particle is minus k times x. A restoring force, always tugging it home, and that is the true definition of simple harmonic motion. So the swing was never magic. Anything pulled back toward a center by a force that grows with distance will swing in simple harmonic motion, from a pendulum to a vibrating guitar string.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_2:spring_block_oscillation>> Why does a block on a spring keep overshooting the very place it's trying to get back to? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's our setup: <<FOCUS:block>> a small block on a perfectly smooth, <<FOCUS:table>> frictionless table, <<FOCUS:spring+wall>> tied to the wall by a spring. <<SECTION:The center point|id=sec-1>> When the spring is at its natural length, neither stretched nor squeezed, the block just sits here, at <<FOCUS:point-O>> a point we'll call O. <<WRITE_TEXT:x = displacement from O|id=text-1>> Now grab the block and pull it to the right, <<FOCUS:point-P>> out to a point P, stretching the spring. That distance from O is <<FOCUS:displacement-x>> the displacement, x. The stretched spring pulls back, and here is the heart of it: that pull <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> always points back toward O, and it gets stronger the further out you go. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force always points toward O, F = -kx|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So at every instant the force is proportional to the displacement but pointing the opposite way. That single rule is what we call simple harmonic motion. <<PAUSE:short>> The force equals the spring constant times the displacement, <<FOCUS:F-label>> with a minus sign because it always points back toward the center. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F = -kx|id=eq-1|boxed>> Let go at P, and the force <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> drags the block toward O. <<UNFOCUS>> With nothing slowing it, the block speeds up the whole way in. But watch what happens <<FOCUS:point-O>> right at O. <<UNFOCUS>> The spring is back to natural length, so the force is zero, yet the block is now moving as fast as it ever will. So if there's no force pulling it any further, why doesn't the block just stop at O? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because it's moving fast. A moving thing keeps moving, so it sails straight through the center and now squeezes the spring on the other side. Now the compressed spring shoves it back, slowing it down, until it <<FOCUS:point-Q>> stops dead at Q, exactly as far out as P was, and the whole journey reverses. <<WRITE_KEY:Fastest at center, momentarily still at the ends|id=key-2>> That's the rhythm: <<FOCUS:point-O>> fastest at the center where the force is zero, momentarily <<FOCUS:point-P+point-Q>> frozen at the ends where the force is strongest. <<UNFOCUS>> The overshoot happens precisely because at O the block is moving its fastest, not its slowest. <<PAUSE:short>> And that endless trade between speed at the middle and pull at the edges is the qualitative signature of every simple harmonic motion you'll ever meet. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_3:shm_line>> Pull a mass on a spring, let go, and it doesn't just snap back and stop — it overshoots, comes back, and overshoots again. One tiny minus sign is the reason it wiggles forever. <<FOCUS:particle>> Here's our particle of mass m, sliding along <<FOCUS:x-axis>> a line we'll call the X-axis, and <<FOCUS:origin>> right at the center sits the origin, the home it keeps trying to return to. <<SECTION:The restoring force|id=sec-1>> One special force acts on it, and <<FOCUS:restoring-force>> watch the arrow: wherever the particle is, the force points straight back toward the center. The force is always proportional to how far the particle has strayed, and <<FOCUS:restoring-force+origin>> it points the opposite way — back toward the center. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F = -kx|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:F = -kx, minus = points home|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> In symbols the force equals negative k times x, where k is positive and x is the distance from home. The farther it wanders, the harder it gets pulled back — and that minus sign is the whole secret. <<PAUSE:short>> Now force divided by mass gives acceleration, so the acceleration equals negative k over m times x. To keep the math tidy we rename k over m as omega squared. <<PAUSE:short>> Dividing the force by the mass gives acceleration, and we rename k over m as omega squared to keep things clean. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = -\frac{k}{m}x = -\omega^2 x|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:a = -omega^2 x : the signature of SHM|id=key-1>> So acceleration equals negative omega squared times displacement. That single line is the fingerprint of every simple harmonic motion in the universe. <<PAUSE:short>> But here's the honest question: knowing the acceleration at every point, can we figure out how fast the particle is actually moving at each spot along the line? <<PAUSE:long>> Using a chain-rule trick we trade the time derivative for one in displacement, so velocity and position sit on opposite sides ready to add up. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v\,dv = -\omega^2 x\,dx|id=eq-3|boxed>> We use a neat trick — acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, but with the chain rule we can rewrite it so velocity sits with position. That gives v times dv equals negative omega squared times x times dx. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Sum from center (x=0) out to x|id=step-1>> Now we add up all those tiny pieces from the center, where the speed is biggest, all the way out to position x. Adding them up — integrating — gives the velocity at every single point. Adding up all those tiny changes from the center out to position x gives the velocity at every point, where A is the farthest the particle ever reaches. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}|id=eq-4|boxed>> The particle can <<FOCUS:amplitude-right>> only reach so far before it stops and turns around. Call that farthest distance A, the amplitude. And the same on the other side — it <<FOCUS:amplitude-left>> swings out to minus A and no farther. <<WRITE_KEY:v = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2)|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the velocity equals omega times the square root of A squared minus x squared. At the edges, <<FOCUS:amplitude-right>> where x equals A, the speed is zero — it's turning around. <<FOCUS:origin>> At the center, where x is zero, it's flat out fastest. <<PAUSE:short>> So that one little minus sign in the force gives us everything: <<FOCUS:restoring-force>> a pull that always points home, an acceleration shaped like negative omega squared x, and a velocity that peaks at the center and dies at the edges. <<UNFOCUS>> That's simple harmonic motion, fully described.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_4>>
A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_4:shm_displacement_graph>> Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by <<TRACE:sine-curve>> the very same shape, a sine curve. <<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:displacement-axis>> The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and <<FOCUS:time-axis>> the horizontal axis is time ticking forward. <<UNFOCUS>> Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less. So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, <<FOCUS:crest-point>> reaching the crest here and <<FOCUS:trough-point>> the trough here. <<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>> That height, from the center out to the crest, <<FOCUS:amplitude-line+amplitude-label>> is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = max displacement from center|id=text-1>> Make the swing bigger or smaller and only A changes; the shape stays a perfect sine. Amplitude is the size of the motion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>> But amplitude alone is not enough. Two pendulums can swing the same distance, yet one is lazy and slow while the other is frantic and fast. So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction. <<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>> The time for that one complete oscillation <<FOCUS:period-bracket+period-label>> is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin(\omega t + \delta) = \sin[\omega(t + T) + \delta]|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass two hundred grams, that's two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion. The restoring force is provided by a spring of spring constant eighty newtons per meter. We need to find the time period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 200 g, k = 80 N/m. Find the time period T.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the square root, two hundred times ten to the minus three divided by eighty gives a square root of zero point zero five seconds. So T equals two pi times zero point zero five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π × 0.05 s|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is zero point three one seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 0.31 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude A along the X-axis. At time t equals zero, the position of the particle is x equals A over two, and it moves along the positive x direction. We want to find the phase constant delta, given that the equation is written as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: SHM amplitude A. At t=0, x = A/2 moving in +x direction. Find phase constant delta for x = A sin(omega t + delta).|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the position equation, x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the position is x equals A over two. <<WRITE_STEP:x = A sin(omega t + delta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So we substitute and get A over two equals A sine delta, which means sine delta equals one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A/2 = A sin(delta)  =>  sin(delta) = 1/2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>> The velocity is the derivative of position, so v equals A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the velocity is A omega cosine delta, and since the particle moves in the positive x direction, this must be positive. <<WRITE_STEP:v = A*omega*cos(omega t + delta);  at t=0, v = A*omega*cos(delta) > 0|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now compare the two candidates: cosine of pi over six is positive, equal to root three over two, while cosine of five pi over six is negative, equal to minus root three over two. Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>> And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>> Because the motion truly repeats, the particle must be at the same place with the same velocity at time t and again at time t plus T, which is what fixes the period. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = how big, T = how often|id=text-2>> So there it is: amplitude tells you how big the swing is, and the time period tells you how often it repeats. Two numbers, and you can rebuild the motion.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_5>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_5:circle_projection>> Watch the shadow of a spinning ball on a wall. The ball circles at a perfectly steady speed, but its shadow speeds up, slows down, stops dead, and races back the other way. Let's build that picture exactly. Here is <<FOCUS:particle-p+circle>> a particle P going around a circle of radius A at a constant rate. <<UNFOCUS>> We call that steady spinning rate the angular speed, omega. At the start, when time is zero, <<FOCUS:particle-p+x-axis>> P sits on the X-axis. As time passes, <<TRACE:radius-op>> the radius from the centre to P sweeps round, and the <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> angle it makes with the X-axis is simply omega times t. <<SECTION:The shadow on the X-axis|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now the clever move. From P, <<TRACE:perpendicular-pq>> drop a straight line down onto the X-axis. The point <<FOCUS:foot-q>> where it lands, Q, is the particle's shadow. <<UNFOCUS>> As P races round the top of the circle, watch only Q. Where is Q moving fastest, and where does it momentarily stop? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> At the edges, near the far left and far right, P is moving almost straight up or down, so <<FOCUS:foot-q>> its shadow Q barely shifts and stops for an instant. <<UNFOCUS>> Near the centre, P moves sideways, so Q sweeps through fastest. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Shadow Q is fastest at the centre, frozen at the edges|id=key-1>> That stopping at the ends and racing through the middle — that is exactly the rhythm of simple harmonic motion, even though P never changes its speed. <<PAUSE:short>> So how far is Q from the centre? Look at the right triangle made by <<FOCUS:radius-op+angle-theta+perpendicular-pq>> the radius OP, the angle omega t, and the horizontal distance to Q. <<WRITE_STEP:OQ is the adjacent side, OP is the hypotenuse A|id=step-1>> <<FOCUS:foot-q>> The distance OQ is the adjacent side, and <<FOCUS:radius-op>> the radius A is the hypotenuse. <<UNFOCUS>> So OQ equals A times the cosine of the angle. <<PAUSE:short>> The shadow's distance from the centre is the radius times the cosine of the angle it has turned through. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\cos\omega t|id=eq-1|boxed>> Since the angle is omega t, the position of the shadow is x equals A cosine omega t. That is the equation of simple harmonic motion, with amplitude A and angular frequency omega. <<PAUSE:short>> And if we drop the perpendicular <<FOCUS:y-axis>> onto the Y-axis instead, that shadow follows y equals A sine omega t — the very same back-and-forth, just a quarter turn out of step. <<UNFOCUS>> The shadow on the perpendicular axis is the radius times the sine of the same angle. <<WRITE_EQUATION:y = A\sin\omega t|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Projection of circular motion onto a diameter = SHM|id=key-2>> So here is the whole idea in one line: the shadow of steady circular motion, cast onto any diameter, is simple harmonic motion. Circles and oscillations are secretly the same thing. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_6>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_6:shm_energy_bars>> A mass on a spring <<FOCUS:edge-line>> freezes for an instant at each edge, then <<FOCUS:centre-line>> whips through the middle at top speed — and yet it never loses a single joule. <<UNFOCUS>> Where does the energy go and come back from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Potential energy in SHM|id=sec-1>> The restoring force in simple harmonic motion always pulls back toward the centre, and its strength grows the further out you go. <<WRITE_TEXT:Work to stretch out = stored energy|id=text-1>> To drag the mass outward you have to fight that force, and the work you spend gets <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> stored as potential energy in the spring. Adding up that work from the centre out to a position x gives a potential energy of one half k x squared — small near the middle, <<FOCUS:pe-bar+edge-line>> largest at the very edge. <<UNFOCUS>> The potential energy stored at displacement x is one half k x squared, which we can also write as one half m omega squared x squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:U(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SECTION:Kinetic energy fills the gap|id=sec-2>> Now <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> watch the kinetic energy: it does the exact opposite, <<FOCUS:ke-bar+centre-line>> peaking at the centre where the mass moves fastest and dropping to zero at the edges. So at the centre it is <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> all kinetic and no potential, and at the edge it is <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> all potential and no kinetic — the two are forever trading places. <<PAUSE:short>> If <<FOCUS:pe-bar+ke-bar>> one bar always rises exactly as much as the other one falls, what must happen to their sum? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Total energy stays constant in SHM|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> The sum stays flat. Every joule the potential gains, the kinetic gives up — so <<FOCUS:total-bar>> the total energy bar never changes height as the mass swings. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> We can prove it cleanly. The position varies as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta, and the velocity as A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_STEP:Add U and K, use sin squared plus cos squared equals one|id=step-1>> Plug those into the two energies, add them, and the sine squared and cosine squared collapse to one — the time completely vanishes. Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass forty grams, that's forty times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude two point zero centimeters, which is two point zero times ten to the minus two meters. The time period is zero point two zero seconds, and we want the total mechanical energy of the system. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 40 g, A = 2.0 cm, T = 0.20 s. Find total mechanical energy E.|id=ex-q-1>> Adding the kinetic and potential energies, everything time-dependent cancels and the total energy is just one half m omega squared A squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = U + K = \tfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start from the total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator, E equals one half m omega squared A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, omega equals two pi over T, so we substitute that in. The one half and the square of two pi combine to give two pi squared, and the T squared moves to the denominator, so E equals two pi squared m A squared over T squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (1/2) m (2 pi / T)^2 A^2 = 2 pi^2 m A^2 / T^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Plugging in the numbers, that's two pi squared times forty times ten to the minus three kilograms, times two point zero times ten to the minus two meters squared, all divided by zero point two zero seconds squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 2 pi^2 (40 x 10^-3 kg)(2.0 x 10^-2 m)^2 / (0.20 s)^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Working that out, the total mechanical energy of the system is seven point nine times ten to the minus three joules. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 7.9 x 10^-3 J|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:E = one half m omega squared A squared|id=key-2>> What is left is one half m omega squared A squared. The total energy depends only on the amplitude, never on the instant you look. <<PAUSE:short>> So the spring is just a perfect accountant: it shuffles energy between motion and stretch endlessly, but the books always balance to the same total. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_7>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_7:twisting_umbrella>> Push a hanging umbrella gently to one side, let go, and watch it twist back and forth, over and over, like a clock that can't make up its mind. <<SECTION:Angular SHM|id=sec-1>> It isn't sliding along a line like a block on a spring; it's <<FOCUS:axis>> rotating about a fixed axis, swinging through angles instead of distances. There's one special angle where the body just sits still if you leave it there, <<FOCUS:rest-line>> the rest position, and we call that angle zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:Rest position: net torque = 0|id=text-1>> At that rest position the total twisting force, <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> the torque, is exactly zero, so nothing makes it turn. Now turn it away from rest <<FOCUS:twisted-line>> by some angle theta, and watch what wakes up. Here is <<FOCUS:theta-arc>> the angle theta, measuring how far we twisted the body from its resting line. <<UNFOCUS>> So if we twist it, what does the body actually do when we let go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> A torque appears that fights the twist, pulling the body back toward rest, and the further you turn it, the harder that torque pulls. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque = -k theta (always pulls back to rest)|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That restoring torque is proportional to the angle and always points back home, and that single rule is what makes the motion angular simple harmonic. <<PAUSE:short>> The restoring torque <<FOCUS:torque-label>> equals a stiffness constant times the angle, with a minus sign because it always points back toward rest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = -k\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> Look closely: this is exactly the spring story, but where the spring pulled along a line, <<FOCUS:restoring-torque+theta-arc>> here the torque pulls around an angle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A body makes angular simple harmonic motion with amplitude theta-naught equal to pi over ten radians, and a time period of zero point zero five seconds. At time zero, the body is at a displacement theta equal to pi over ten radians. We want to write the equation giving the angular displacement as a function of time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Angular SHM, amplitude = pi/10 rad, period = 0.05 s, theta = pi/10 rad at t = 0. Find theta(t).|id=ex-q-1>> The angular acceleration is just the torque divided by the moment of inertia, which gives the same shape as the spring equation with omega squared standing in for k over I. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\omega^2\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start by assuming the general form of the equation. Let theta equal theta-naught times sine of omega t plus delta. Here the amplitude theta-naught is given as pi over ten radians. <<WRITE_STEP:theta = theta-naught sin(omega t + delta), theta-naught = pi/10 rad|id=ex-step-1-1>> Because the equation is identical to the spring's, the angle traces out a sine wave in time swinging between plus and minus its maximum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\theta = \theta_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-3|boxed>> Next we find the angular frequency. Omega equals two pi divided by the period, that is two pi over zero point zero five seconds, which gives forty pi per second. So now theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus delta. <<WRITE_STEP:omega = 2*pi / T = 2*pi / 0.05 = 40*pi per second|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we use the starting condition to find the phase constant delta. At time zero the displacement is pi over ten radians. Putting time equal to zero, pi over ten equals pi over ten times sine of delta. This gives sine of delta equals one, so delta equals pi over two. <<WRITE_STEP:At t=0: pi/10 = (pi/10) sin(delta) => sin(delta) = 1 => delta = pi/2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Substituting delta equals pi over two, theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus pi over two, which simplifies to a cosine. So the final equation is theta equals pi over ten radians times cosine of forty pi times t. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = (pi/10 rad) cos(40*pi t)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Divide torque by moment of inertia I to get angular acceleration|id=step-1>> Divide that torque by the body's moment of inertia, its resistance to being spun, and you get the angular acceleration. And out pops the very same equation as the spring, just with theta in place of x and moment of inertia in place of mass, so the body swings as a smooth sine wave in time. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_8>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_8:pendulum_forces>> Why does a pendulum take exactly the same time to swing whether you pull it back a little or a lot? <<PAUSE:long>> Here is our pendulum: <<FOCUS:bob>> a heavy little ball on a light string, <<FOCUS:pivot>> fixed at the top at point O. <<SECTION:The Simple Pendulum|id=sec-1>> When the string hangs straight down, that is the resting position, where <<FOCUS:equilibrium-line>> the angle theta is zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta equals zero is rest|id=text-1>> Pull the ball aside <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> to some angle theta and let go, and it swings back and forth along a curved arc. Only two forces act on the ball: <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> its weight pulling straight down, and <<FOCUS:tension-vector>> the tension in the string. Now here is the clever part: the tension points exactly along the string, straight back to the pivot, so it can never twist the ball around that pivot. <<UNFOCUS>> It creates no turning effect at all. That leaves the weight alone to do the work. We split it: one part pulls along the string, and one part <<FOCUS:restoring-component>> pulls along the arc, back toward the resting position. That part along the arc is the restoring pull, and its size is <<FOCUS:restoring-label>> the weight times the sine of theta. <<UNFOCUS>> The further you swing out, the stronger it tugs you back. <<WRITE_TEXT:restoring force along arc grows with sine theta|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> The turning effect of the weight about the pivot equals the weight, m g, times the length of the string, times the sine of the angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = mgl\sin\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> But sine of theta is messy. So is this really simple harmonic motion, where the restoring pull must be proportional to the angle itself? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the secret: when the angle is small, the sine of theta is almost exactly equal to theta. The curve and the straight line agree. That tiny approximation is what turns a real swing into perfect simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_KEY:For small angles, sine theta is approximately theta, so the swing is simple harmonic|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Once the restoring pull is proportional to theta, the swing has a fixed rhythm, and its period depends only on the length of the string and on gravity. <<WRITE_KEY:Period depends only on length and gravity, not mass or amplitude|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> The time for one full swing equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> So a heavy ball and a light ball on the same string keep the same time, and a small pull and a big pull keep the same time. That is why a pendulum makes such a beautiful clock. <<WRITE_TEXT:same length, same time|id=text-3>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_9>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_9:physical_pendulum>> Forget the string and the little bob for a second. What if I just grabbed a metal ring, hooked it over a nail, and gave it a push? Does that swing like a pendulum too? <<PAUSE:long>> It does. And here's the big idea: <<SECTION:Physical Pendulum|id=sec-1>> any rigid body, <<FOCUS:pivot-O+body-outline>> hung from a fixed point and left to swing, is what we call a physical pendulum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Inside every object there's one special point, the centre of mass, where all its weight effectively acts. Here it is, <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass-C>> point C. When <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass-C+vertical-line>> C hangs straight down below the pivot, the body just sits there, perfectly balanced. That's the resting position, <<FOCUS:vertical-line>> where the angle is zero. Now <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> pull it aside by an angle we call theta, and <<FOCUS:line-OC>> the line from the pivot to the centre of mass tilts away from straight down. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta = angle of OC from vertical|id=text-1>> This angle theta <<FOCUS:angle-theta+vertical-line+line-OC>> between the vertical and the line to the centre of mass is the whole story. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what gravity does with it. Gravity <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> pulls the centre of mass straight down with a force m g. But notice it's pulling <<FOCUS:weight-vector+pivot-O>> off to the side of the pivot, not through it. <<UNFOCUS>> So here's the question: a force pulling to the side of a pivot, what does it create? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> A torque. A twist that tries to rotate the body back towards the resting position. <<WRITE_KEY:Restoring torque = m g l sine theta|id=key-1>> Its size is the weight m g, times <<FOCUS:line-OC>> the distance l from pivot to centre of mass, times the sine of theta. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The restoring torque equals the weight m g, times the distance l from the pivot to the centre of mass, times the sine of the angle theta, and the minus sign means it always points back towards rest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tau = -mgl\sin\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> And because it always pulls back towards zero, it's a restoring torque, exactly the ingredient we need for oscillation. The <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass-C+weight-vector>> gravity acting at the centre of mass, a distance l away, is what makes the whole rigid body swing. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A uniform rod of length one point zero zero meters is suspended through one end and set into small amplitude oscillation under gravity. We want to find the time period of oscillation. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Rod of length 1.00 m, suspended at one end, oscillates with small amplitude. Find the time period.|id=ex-q-1>> For small angles, sine theta is almost exactly theta, so the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration equals minus m g l times theta, which is the signature of simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -mgl\sin\theta \approx -mgl\,\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> For a small amplitude the angular motion is nearly simple harmonic, so we use the physical pendulum formula: T equals two pi times the square root of I over m g l. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgl}}|id=ex-eq-1>> The period equals two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia I divided by m g l. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgl}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Now we plug in the pieces. The moment of inertia of a rod about an end is m times L squared over three, and the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass is L over two. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√[ (mL²/3) / (mg · L/2) ]|id=ex-step-1-1>> The mass m cancels top and bottom, and one factor of L cancels too, leaving T equals two pi times the square root of two L over three g. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√(2L / 3g)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substitute L equals one point zero zero meters and gravity equals nine point eight zero meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√[ (2 × 1.00) / (3 × 9.80) ]|id=ex-step-1-3>> Working that out gives the time period. And the answer is one point six four seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 1.64 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> <<SET_PARAM:theta|value=8.0>> Now there's a wrinkle. The torque depends on sine theta, not theta itself, so strictly this isn't simple harmonic motion. But for small swings, sine theta is almost exactly theta, and the motion becomes beautifully simple. <<WRITE_KEY:T = 2 pi sqrt(I / m g l)|id=key-2>> When the dust settles, the period comes out as two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia I, divided by m g l. That single formula governs any rigid body you care to hang up and swing. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_10>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_10:torsional_pendulum>> Twist a disc hanging from a thin wire, let go, and watch what happens. It doesn't just snap back to rest. It overshoots, twists the other way, and keeps going back and forth. <<SECTION:Torsional Pendulum|id=sec-1>> Here is the setup. <<FOCUS:disc+wire>> A flat disc hangs from a light wire. The top of the wire is <<FOCUS:support>> clamped firmly to a fixed support, and the wire stays perfectly vertical the whole time. Now instead of swinging it sideways like an ordinary pendulum, we rotate the disc about <<FOCUS:axis>> the wire itself as the axis. <<UNFOCUS>> The bottom of the wire turns with the disc, but the top is held fixed. <<WRITE_TEXT:Wire winds up like a twisted band|id=text-1>> So <<FOCUS:wire>> a twist builds up inside the wire, like winding up a rubber band. We rotate the disc <<FOCUS:twist-angle>> through an angle we call theta. <<UNFOCUS>> And here is the heart of it. The wire hates being twisted. It pushes back, trying to untwist itself and bring the disc home. That push-back <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> is a restoring torque. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now I want you to predict something. If I twist the disc twice as far, how much harder does the wire push back? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Exactly twice as hard. The restoring torque is <<FOCUS:restoring-torque+twist-angle>> directly proportional to the angle of twist. <<UNFOCUS>> Double the twist, double the push-back. That single fact is what makes this motion a clock. <<PAUSE:short>> The torque equals minus the torsional constant times the angle of twist, always pointing back toward zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tau = -k\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Restoring torque tau equals minus k theta|id=key-1>> We write this as: torque equals minus k times theta. The minus sign means it always points back toward zero twist, and k is the torsional constant, a measure of how stiff the wire is. <<PAUSE:short>> Compare this to a stretched spring, where the pull is minus k times the stretch. This is the rotational twin: a restoring effect proportional to displacement. That is the exact signature of simple harmonic motion. <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>> Newton's second law for rotation says torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Substituting our restoring torque gives an angular acceleration always pointing back to centre and proportional to the angle. The angular acceleration is minus k over I times the angle, always pointing back to centre. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\alpha = -\frac{k}{I}\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:Angular acceleration equals minus k over I times theta|id=step-1>> That means the angular frequency squared, omega squared, equals k divided by I. The whole oscillation is set by just two numbers. So how long is one full back-and-forth? It depends only on how stiff the wire is, k, and how hard the disc is to spin, its moment of inertia I. <<PAUSE:short>> The time period is two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{k}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:T equals two pi root I over k|id=key-2>> The time period is two pi times the square root of I over k. A heavier disc swings slower; a stiffer wire swings faster. Notice the angle of twist is nowhere in there, so the period stays the same whether you twist it a little or a lot. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_11>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_11:two_shm_vector_sum>> Suppose a single particle feels two separate springy forces at the same time, each one tugging it back and forth. What on earth does it actually do? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's the trap your brain falls into: you imagine the two motions fighting, tangling up into some hopeless mess that you'd need new physics to describe. But the answer is astonishingly simple, and it falls right out of Newton's second law. Let's just play fair and ask one force at a time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:One force at a time|id=sec-1>> Pretend only the first force acts. By itself it gives the particle some position; call that position r one. Now pretend instead that only the second force acts. By itself it would put the particle at a different position; call that r two. Newton's second law for each force on its own says mass times the acceleration of that position equals that single force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2 r_1}{dt^2} = F_1, \qquad m\frac{d^2 r_2}{dt^2} = F_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> So if I solve each motion on its own, where does the particle really go when both forces act together at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Actual position r equals r1 plus r2, as vectors|id=key-1>> Watch. The real position is simply r one plus r two, tip to tail, the vector sum. Nothing fights, nothing tangles. <<PAUSE:short>> Why is nature this kind to us? Because Newton's second law adds. The mass times acceleration from the first equation, plus the same from the second, must equal the total force. <<PAUSE:short>> And when you add those two equations, the left side becomes the acceleration of r one plus r two, while the right side becomes the resultant force. So that sum r one plus r two is exactly the true motion. <<PAUSE:short>> Adding the two equations, the mass times the acceleration of the sum r one plus r two equals the total of both forces, which is the real resultant force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}(r_1 + r_2) = F_1 + F_2|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Velocities add too: u equals u1 plus u2|id=text-1>> The very same trick works for velocities. The real velocity is the velocity from force one plus the velocity from force two, added as vectors. So the actual position is the vector sum of the two separate positions, and the actual velocity is the vector sum of the two separate velocities. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{r} = \vec{r_1} + \vec{r_2}, \qquad \vec{u} = \vec{u_1} + \vec{u_2}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have two simple harmonic motions along the x-axis with the same frequency. The first has an amplitude of two point zero centimeters, and the second also has an amplitude of two point zero centimeters. The phase difference between them is pi over three, which is sixty degrees. We want the amplitude of the combined motion. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Combine x1 = (2.0 cm) sin wt and x2 = (2.0 cm) sin(wt + pi/3); find resultant amplitude|id=ex-q-1>> Since both motions are along the same direction, we combine their amplitudes using the resultant amplitude formula: A equals the square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus two times A one times A two times cosine of delta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2 A_1 A_2 \cos\delta}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we substitute the values. A one is two point zero centimeters, A two is two point zero centimeters, and delta is pi over three. <<WRITE_STEP:A = sqrt[(2.0 cm)^2 + (2.0 cm)^2 + 2(2.0 cm)^2 cos(pi/3)]|id=ex-step-1-1>> The cosine of pi over three equals one half, so the last term becomes two times two point zero squared times one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A = sqrt[4.0 + 4.0 + 2(4.0)(1/2)] cm = sqrt[12.0] cm|indent=1|id=ex-step-1-2>> Taking the square root, the resultant amplitude comes out to three point five centimeters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A = 3.5 cm|id=ex-ans-1>> This shortcut has a famous name, the principle of superposition. Solve each simple harmonic motion in peace, then just add the answers. So two forces at once never need new physics. The actual position is the vector sum of where each force alone would have placed it, and that is the whole secret. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_12>>
Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still. Up to now we pretended a swing keeps the same size forever, swinging back and forth with a steady amplitude, driven only by a restoring force pulling it toward the center. <<SECTION:The damping force|id=sec-1>> But the real world has a second force, a brake, and we call it the damping force. Friction, air resistance, anything that resists motion. Here is its defining habit: the damping force always points opposite to the velocity. Whichever way the object moves, this force pushes back against it. <<PAUSE:short>> The braking force points opposite to the velocity, and for many real cases its size is just proportional to how fast the thing is moving. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{damp}} = -bv|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:damping force opposes velocity|id=text-1>> And in many real situations its strength is simply proportional to the speed, so we write the damping force as minus b times v. Now, a force that always opposes the velocity does negative work on the object every single moment of the motion. Negative work means it steadily removes energy. <<PAUSE:short>> So here is the honest question: if energy keeps leaking out swing after swing, what happens to the size of the swing over time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_12:damped_oscillation_curve>> Each swing carries a little less energy than the last, so each swing reaches a little less far. <<FOCUS:oscillation-curve>> The amplitude shrinks, swing after swing, until the motion dies. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The decaying envelope|id=sec-2>> <<FOCUS:first-peak>> Watch the peaks. They sit inside <<FOCUS:envelope-upper+envelope-lower>> two smooth curves that close in toward the center line, an envelope that squeezes the motion down to nothing. The motion is <<FOCUS:oscillation-curve>> still a sine wave, but its amplitude is no longer fixed; it's multiplied by a shrinking exponential that fades the swing away. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A_0\, e^{-\frac{bt}{2m}} \sin(\omega t + \phi)|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:amplitude decays inside a shrinking exponential envelope|id=key-1>> <<FOCUS:first-peak>> The first swing is the tallest, and from there every peak <<TRACE:envelope-upper>> hides beneath a fading exponential curve, all the way down to rest. <<UNFOCUS>> But notice the rhythm between the peaks barely changes. For light damping the system still oscillates with almost its natural frequency, the same frequency it would have with no brake at all. <<PAUSE:short>> So a damped oscillation is two ideas in one picture: the familiar back-and-forth rhythm, riding inside an amplitude that quietly fades to zero, <<FOCUS:rest-point>> right here at the resting point.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_13>>
Soldiers marching in perfect step are ordered to break stride before crossing a bridge. Why would an army be afraid of walking in time? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer is hiding in a single idea: what happens when you keep pushing on something that already likes to swing back and forth. Think of a child on a swing. Left alone after one push, friction and air slowly drain the energy and the swing dies down. <<WRITE_TEXT:Free swing decays to rest|id=text-1>> But now you stand behind and give a gentle push, again and again, on your own rhythm. That repeating outside push is what we call a driving force, and the motion it creates is forced oscillation. <<SECTION:Forced oscillation|id=sec-1>> Here is the surprising part. The swing has its own favourite rhythm, its natural frequency. But push it at a different rhythm, and after a messy moment it gives in and swings at your rhythm, not its own. <<PAUSE:short>> The driver takes charge of the beat. The body ends up oscillating at the frequency of the force you apply. <<WRITE_KEY:Driven body oscillates at the driving frequency, not its natural one|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> And because every push tops up the energy that damping steals away, the swinging no longer dies out. It settles to a steady, constant size. The body feels three things at once: the spring pulling it back, the damping dragging it down, and the outside push that rises and falls with time. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{dv}{dt} = -kx - bv + F_0\sin(\omega t)|id=eq-1|boxed>> So here is the real question: if I can push at any rhythm I like, does it matter which one I choose? Is every rhythm just as good? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_13:resonance_curve>> Watch what happens to the size of the swing as I change my pushing frequency. Here is the <<FOCUS:amplitude-axis>> amplitude plotted <<FOCUS:freq-axis>> against the driving frequency. When my pushing rhythm <<FOCUS:natural-freq-line>> matches the swing's own natural rhythm, the amplitude <<FOCUS:resonance-peak>> shoots up to a peak. <<UNFOCUS>> Pushing in time with its favourite beat pours energy in most efficiently. <<SECTION:Resonance|id=sec-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> This matching condition has a name: resonance. And now look at what damping does to the picture. <<PAUSE:short>> With heavy damping <<FOCUS:curve-heavy-damping>> the peak is low and broad. But with light damping the peak becomes a <<FOCUS:curve-light-damping>> towering, razor-sharp spike, the amplitude growing enormous near the natural frequency. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> We can put numbers on it. The steady amplitude depends on how far your driving frequency sits from the natural frequency, and on the damping. The steady amplitude is large when the driving frequency omega sits <<FOCUS:natural-freq-tick>> close to the natural frequency omega-naught, and it is held in check by the damping term underneath. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now the soldiers make sense. March in step at just the wrong rhythm and you become a driving force on the bridge. Hit its natural frequency, with little damping to save you, and the resonant swing can grow until the bridge tears itself apart. <<WRITE_KEY:Resonance: drive at the natural frequency and amplitude can become huge|id=key-2>>

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We start with the universal observation that things in nature love to repeat — swings, springs, pendulums — and uncover the single mathematical fingerprint they all share: acceleration that always points home and grows with distance. From that one rule (a = -ω²x) we build the full machinery — energy, circular-motion geometry, and every flavor of pendulum — then end by confronting reality, where friction kills oscillations and a well-timed push can amplify them catastrophically.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: A child on a swing, a clock's pendulum, a guitar string, and a skyscraper swaying in the wind all obey the exact same hidden rule. What if one simple equation could describe all of them at once?

coverage_checklist.description: Define periodic/harmonic motion and connect it to everyday examples (swing, clock pendulum) before any math
Establish the defining condition of SHM: restoring force F = -kx and acceleration a = -ω²x, with emphasis on the meaning of the minus sign
Solve the equation of motion to get x = A sin(ωt + φ) and define amplitude, period, frequency, angular frequency, and phase
Show SHM as the projection of uniform circular motion to give geometric intuition for the sine solution
Demonstrate that total mechanical energy stays constant while KE and PE trade back and forth
Extend SHM to rotational/angular systems and pendulums (simple, physical, torsional) and derive their periods
Show what happens to real oscillators: damping drains energy and amplitude decays over time
Explain forced oscillation and resonance — why a matched driving frequency produces huge amplitudes (bridges, tuning, skyscrapers)

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We began by asking how a child's swing, a pendulum clock, a guitar string, and a swaying skyscraper could possibly share one rule — and now you know the answer: whenever the force pulling something back is proportional to its displacement, you get simple harmonic motion, captured by a = -ω²x and described by a clean sine wave. From that single seed grew everything: the period and amplitude that label each oscillation, the elegant link to circular motion, the constant total energy sloshing between kinetic and potential, and the family of pendulums that all reduce to the same idea. Finally we faced reality — damping slowly steals the energy away, while a perfectly timed driving force can pump it back in until resonance builds the motion to dramatic, sometimes destructive, heights. That last idea is why the skyscraper from our opening either sways gently or shakes apart: it all comes down to one equation you now own.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_2:spring_block_oscillation>> Why does a block on a spring keep overshooting the very place it's trying to get back to? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's our setup: <<FOCUS:block>> a small block on a perfectly smooth, <<FOCUS:table>> frictionless table, <<FOCUS:spring+wall>> tied to the wall by a spring. <<SECTION:The center point|id=sec-1>> When the spring is at its natural length, neither stretched nor squeezed, the block just sits here, at <<FOCUS:point-O>> a point we'll call O. <<WRITE_TEXT:x = displacement from O|id=text-1>> Now grab the block and pull it to the right, <<FOCUS:point-P>> out to a point P, stretching the spring. The stretched spring pulls back, and here is the heart of it: that pull <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> always points back toward O, and it gets stronger the further out you go. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force always points toward O, F = -kx|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So at every instant the force is proportional to the displacement but pointing the opposite way. segments.narration_chapter: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_4:shm_displacement_graph>> Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by <<TRACE:sine-curve>> the very same shape, a sine curve. <<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:displacement-axis>> The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and <<FOCUS:time-axis>> the horizontal axis is time ticking forward. <<UNFOCUS>> Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less. So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, <<FOCUS:crest-point>> reaching the crest here and <<FOCUS:trough-point>> the trough here. <<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>> That height, from the center out to the crest, <<FOCUS:amplitude-line+amplitude-label>> is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = max displacement from center|id=text-1>> Make the swing bigger or smaller and only A changes; the shape stays a perfect sine. Amplitude is the size of the motion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>> But amplitude alone is not enough. Two pendulums can swing the same distance, yet one is lazy and slow while the other is frantic and fast. So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction. <<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>> The time for that one complete oscillation <<FOCUS:period-bracket+period-label>> is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin(\omega t + \delta) = \sin[\omega(t + T) + \delta]|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass two hundred grams, that's two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion. The restoring force is provided by a spring of spring constant eighty newtons per meter. We need to find the time period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 200 g, k = 80 N/m. Find the time period T.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the square root, two hundred times ten to the minus three divided by eighty gives a square root of zero point zero five seconds. So T equals two pi times zero point zero five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π × 0.05 s|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is zero point three one seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 0.31 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude A along the X-axis. At time t equals zero, the position of the particle is x equals A over two, and it moves along the positive x direction. We want to find the phase constant delta, given that the equation is written as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: SHM amplitude A. At t=0, x = A/2 moving in +x direction. Find phase constant delta for x = A sin(omega t + delta).|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the position equation, x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the position is x equals A over two. <<WRITE_STEP:x = A sin(omega t + delta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So we substitute and get A over two equals A sine delta, which means sine delta equals one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A/2 = A sin(delta)  =>  sin(delta) = 1/2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>> The velocity is the derivative of position, so v equals A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the velocity is A omega cosine delta, and since the particle moves in the positive x direction, this must be positive. <<WRITE_STEP:v = A*omega*cos(omega t + delta);  at t=0, v = A*omega*cos(delta) > 0|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now compare the two candidates: cosine of pi over six is positive, equal to root three over two, while cosine of five pi over six is negative, equal to minus root three over two. Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>> And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>> Because the motion truly repeats, the particle must be at the same place with the same velocity at time t and again at time t plus T, which is what fixes the period. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = how big, T = how often|id=text-2>> So there it is: amplitude tells you how big the swing is, and the time period tells you how often it repeats. Two numbers, and you can rebuild the motion.
segments.narration_standalone: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_4:shm_displacement_graph>> Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by the very same shape, a sine curve. <<TRACE:sine-curve>> <<FOCUS:displacement-axis>> <<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>>The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and the horizontal axis is time ticking forward. <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less. So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, reaching the crest here and the trough here. <<POINT:crest-point>> <<FOCUS:amplitude-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>>That height, from the center out to the crest, is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle. <<PAUSE:short>> Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:trough-point>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = max displacement from center|id=text-1>>Make the swing bigger or smaller and only A changes; the shape stays a perfect sine. Amplitude is the size of the motion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>>But amplitude alone is not enough. Two pendulums can swing the same distance, yet one is lazy and slow while the other is frantic and fast. <<FOCUS:time-axis>> So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction. <<POINT:period-bracket>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> <<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>>The time for that one complete oscillation is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were. <<PAUSE:short>> For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin(\omega t + \delta) = \sin[\omega(t + T) + \delta]|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass two hundred grams, that's two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion. The restoring force is provided by a spring of spring constant eighty newtons per meter. We need to find the time period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 200 g, k = 80 N/m. Find the time period T.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the square root, two hundred times ten to the minus three divided by eighty gives a square root of zero point zero five seconds. So T equals two pi times zero point zero five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π × 0.05 s|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is zero point three one seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 0.31 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude A along the X-axis. At time t equals zero, the position of the particle is x equals A over two, and it moves along the positive x direction. We want to find the phase constant delta, given that the equation is written as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: SHM amplitude A. At t=0, x = A/2 moving in +x direction. Find phase constant delta for x = A sin(omega t + delta).|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the position equation, x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the position is x equals A over two. <<WRITE_STEP:x = A sin(omega t + delta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So we substitute and get A over two equals A sine delta, which means sine delta equals one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A/2 = A sin(delta)  =>  sin(delta) = 1/2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>> The velocity is the derivative of position, so v equals A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the velocity is A omega cosine delta, and since the particle moves in the positive x direction, this must be positive. <<WRITE_STEP:v = A*omega*cos(omega t + delta);  at t=0, v = A*omega*cos(delta) > 0|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now compare the two candidates: cosine of pi over six is positive, equal to root three over two, while cosine of five pi over six is negative, equal to minus root three over two. Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>> And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> Because the motion truly repeats, the particle must be at the same place with the same velocity at time t and again at time t plus T, which is what fixes the period. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = how big, T = how often|id=text-2>>So there it is: amplitude tells you how big the swing is, and the time period tells you how often it repeats. Two numbers, and you can rebuild the motion.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_5:circle_projection>> Watch the shadow of a spinning ball on a wall. The ball circles at a perfectly steady speed, but its shadow speeds up, slows down, stops dead, and races back the other way. Let's build that picture exactly. Here is <<FOCUS:particle-p+circle>> a particle P going around a circle of radius A at a constant rate. <<UNFOCUS>> We call that steady spinning rate the angular speed, omega. At the start, when time is zero, <<FOCUS:particle-p+x-axis>> P sits on the X-axis. As time passes, <<TRACE:radius-op>> the radius from the centre to P sweeps round, and the <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> angle it makes with the X-axis is simply omega times t. <<SECTION:The shadow on the X-axis|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now the clever move. From P, <<TRACE:perpendicular-pq>> drop a straight line down onto the X-axis. The point <<FOCUS:foot-q>> where it lands, Q, is the particle's shadow. <<UNFOCUS>> As P races round the top of the circle, watch only Q. Where is Q moving fastest, and where does it momentarily stop? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> At the edges, near the far left and far right, P is moving almost straight up or down, so <<FOCUS:foot-q>> its shadow Q barely shifts and stops for an instant. <<UNFOCUS>> Near the centre, P moves sideways, so Q sweeps through fastest. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Shadow Q is fastest at the centre, frozen at the edges|id=key-1>> That stopping at the ends and racing through the middle — that is exactly the rhythm of simple harmonic motion, even though P never changes its speed. <<PAUSE:short>> So how far is Q from the centre? Look at the right triangle made by <<FOCUS:radius-op+angle-theta+perpendicular-pq>> the radius OP, the angle omega t, and the horizontal distance to Q. <<WRITE_STEP:OQ is the adjacent side, OP is the hypotenuse A|id=step-1>> <<FOCUS:foot-q>> The distance OQ is the adjacent side, and <<FOCUS:radius-op>> the radius A is the hypotenuse. <<UNFOCUS>> So OQ equals A times the cosine of the angle. <<PAUSE:short>> The shadow's distance from the centre is the radius times the cosine of the angle it has turned through. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\cos\omega t|id=eq-1|boxed>> Since the angle is omega t, the position of the shadow is x equals A cosine omega t. That is the equation of simple harmonic motion, with amplitude A and angular frequency omega. <<PAUSE:short>> And if we drop the perpendicular <<FOCUS:y-axis>> onto the Y-axis instead, that shadow follows y equals A sine omega t — the very same back-and-forth, just a quarter turn out of step. <<UNFOCUS>> The shadow on the perpendicular axis is the radius times the sine of the same angle. <<WRITE_EQUATION:y = A\sin\omega t|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Projection of circular motion onto a diameter = SHM|id=key-2>> So here is the whole idea in one line: the shadow of steady circular motion, cast onto any diameter, is simple harmonic motion. Circles and oscillations are secretly the same thing. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_6:shm_energy_bars>> A mass on a spring <<FOCUS:edge-line>> freezes for an instant at each edge, then <<FOCUS:centre-line>> whips through the middle at top speed — and yet it never loses a single joule. <<UNFOCUS>> Where does the energy go and come back from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Potential energy in SHM|id=sec-1>> The restoring force in simple harmonic motion always pulls back toward the centre, and its strength grows the further out you go. <<WRITE_TEXT:Work to stretch out = stored energy|id=text-1>> To drag the mass outward you have to fight that force, and the work you spend gets <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> stored as potential energy in the spring. Adding up that work from the centre out to a position x gives a potential energy of one half k x squared — small near the middle, <<FOCUS:pe-bar+edge-line>> largest at the very edge. <<UNFOCUS>> The potential energy stored at displacement x is one half k x squared, which we can also write as one half m omega squared x squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:U(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SECTION:Kinetic energy fills the gap|id=sec-2>> Now <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> watch the kinetic energy: it does the exact opposite, <<FOCUS:ke-bar+centre-line>> peaking at the centre where the mass moves fastest and dropping to zero at the edges. So at the centre it is <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> all kinetic and no potential, and at the edge it is <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> all potential and no kinetic — the two are forever trading places. <<PAUSE:short>> If <<FOCUS:pe-bar+ke-bar>> one bar always rises exactly as much as the other one falls, what must happen to their sum? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Total energy stays constant in SHM|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> The sum stays flat. Every joule the potential gains, the kinetic gives up — so <<FOCUS:total-bar>> the total energy bar never changes height as the mass swings. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> We can prove it cleanly. The position varies as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta, and the velocity as A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_STEP:Add U and K, use sin squared plus cos squared equals one|id=step-1>> Plug those into the two energies, add them, and the sine squared and cosine squared collapse to one — the time completely vanishes. Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass forty grams, that's forty times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude two point zero centimeters, which is two point zero times ten to the minus two meters. The time period is zero point two zero seconds, and we want the total mechanical energy of the system. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 40 g, A = 2.0 cm, T = 0.20 s. Find total mechanical energy E.|id=ex-q-1>> Adding the kinetic and potential energies, everything time-dependent cancels and the total energy is just one half m omega squared A squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:E = U + K = \tfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 A^2|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start from the total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator, E equals one half m omega squared A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, omega equals two pi over T, so we substitute that in. The one half and the square of two pi combine to give two pi squared, and the T squared moves to the denominator, so E equals two pi squared m A squared over T squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (1/2) m (2 pi / T)^2 A^2 = 2 pi^2 m A^2 / T^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Plugging in the numbers, that's two pi squared times forty times ten to the minus three kilograms, times two point zero times ten to the minus two meters squared, all divided by zero point two zero seconds squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 2 pi^2 (40 x 10^-3 kg)(2.0 x 10^-2 m)^2 / (0.20 s)^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Working that out, the total mechanical energy of the system is seven point nine times ten to the minus three joules. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 7.9 x 10^-3 J|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:E = one half m omega squared A squared|id=key-2>> What is left is one half m omega squared A squared. The total energy depends only on the amplitude, never on the instant you look. <<PAUSE:short>> So the spring is just a perfect accountant: it shuffles energy between motion and stretch endlessly, but the books always balance to the same total. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_7:twisting_umbrella>> Push a hanging umbrella gently to one side, let go, and watch it twist back and forth, over and over, like a clock that can't make up its mind. <<SECTION:Angular SHM|id=sec-1>> It isn't sliding along a line like a block on a spring; it's <<FOCUS:axis>> rotating about a fixed axis, swinging through angles instead of distances. There's one special angle where the body just sits still if you leave it there, <<FOCUS:rest-line>> the rest position, and we call that angle zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:Rest position: net torque = 0|id=text-1>> At that rest position the total twisting force, <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> the torque, is exactly zero, so nothing makes it turn. Now turn it away from rest <<FOCUS:twisted-line>> by some angle theta, and watch what wakes up. Here is <<FOCUS:theta-arc>> the angle theta, measuring how far we twisted the body from its resting line. <<UNFOCUS>> So if we twist it, what does the body actually do when we let go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> A torque appears that fights the twist, pulling the body back toward rest, and the further you turn it, the harder that torque pulls. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque = -k theta (always pulls back to rest)|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That restoring torque is proportional to the angle and always points back home, and that single rule is what makes the motion angular simple harmonic. <<PAUSE:short>> The restoring torque <<FOCUS:torque-label>> equals a stiffness constant times the angle, with a minus sign because it always points back toward rest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = -k\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> Look closely: this is exactly the spring story, but where the spring pulled along a line, <<FOCUS:restoring-torque+theta-arc>> here the torque pulls around an angle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A body makes angular simple harmonic motion with amplitude theta-naught equal to pi over ten radians, and a time period of zero point zero five seconds. At time zero, the body is at a displacement theta equal to pi over ten radians. We want to write the equation giving the angular displacement as a function of time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Angular SHM, amplitude = pi/10 rad, period = 0.05 s, theta = pi/10 rad at t = 0. Find theta(t).|id=ex-q-1>> The angular acceleration is just the torque divided by the moment of inertia, which gives the same shape as the spring equation with omega squared standing in for k over I. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\omega^2\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start by assuming the general form of the equation. Let theta equal theta-naught times sine of omega t plus delta. Here the amplitude theta-naught is given as pi over ten radians. <<WRITE_STEP:theta = theta-naught sin(omega t + delta), theta-naught = pi/10 rad|id=ex-step-1-1>> Because the equation is identical to the spring's, the angle traces out a sine wave in time swinging between plus and minus its maximum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\theta = \theta_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-3|boxed>> Next we find the angular frequency. Omega equals two pi divided by the period, that is two pi over zero point zero five seconds, which gives forty pi per second. So now theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus delta. <<WRITE_STEP:omega = 2*pi / T = 2*pi / 0.05 = 40*pi per second|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we use the starting condition to find the phase constant delta. At time zero the displacement is pi over ten radians. Putting time equal to zero, pi over ten equals pi over ten times sine of delta. This gives sine of delta equals one, so delta equals pi over two. <<WRITE_STEP:At t=0: pi/10 = (pi/10) sin(delta) => sin(delta) = 1 => delta = pi/2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Substituting delta equals pi over two, theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus pi over two, which simplifies to a cosine. So the final equation is theta equals pi over ten radians times cosine of forty pi times t. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = (pi/10 rad) cos(40*pi t)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Divide torque by moment of inertia I to get angular acceleration|id=step-1>> Divide that torque by the body's moment of inertia, its resistance to being spun, and you get the angular acceleration. And out pops the very same equation as the spring, just with theta in place of x and moment of inertia in place of mass, so the body swings as a smooth sine wave in time. <<PAUSE:short>>
