There's one special angle where the body just sits still if you leave it there, the rest position, and we call that angle zero. <<TRACE:rest-line>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Rest position: net torque = 0|id=text-1>>At that rest position the total twisting force, the torque, is exactly zero, so nothing makes it turn. <<POINT:rest-line>> <<FOCUS:twisted-line>> Now turn it away from rest by some angle theta, and watch what wakes up. <<TRACE:twisted-line>> Here is the angle theta, measuring how far we twisted the body from its resting line. <<TRACE:theta-arc>> <<FOCUS:twisted-line>> So if we twist it, what does the body actually do when we let go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> A torque appears that fights the twist, pulling the body back toward rest, and the further you turn it, the harder that torque pulls. <<TRACE:restoring-torque>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque = -k theta (always pulls back to rest)|id=key-1>>That restoring torque is proportional to the angle and always points back home, and that single rule is what makes the motion angular simple harmonic. <<PAUSE:short>> The restoring torque equals a stiffness constant times the angle, with a minus sign because it always points back toward rest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = -k\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:theta-arc>> Look closely: this is exactly the spring story, but where the spring pulled along a line, here the torque pulls around an angle. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. A body makes angular simple harmonic motion with amplitude theta-naught equal to pi over ten radians, and a time period of zero point zero five seconds. At time zero, the body is at a displacement theta equal to pi over ten radians. We want to write the equation giving the angular displacement as a function of time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Angular SHM, amplitude = pi/10 rad, period = 0.05 s, theta = pi/10 rad at t = 0. Find theta(t).|id=ex-q-1>> The angular acceleration is just the torque divided by the moment of inertia, which gives the same shape as the spring equation with omega squared standing in for k over I. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -\omega^2\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start by assuming the general form of the equation. Let theta equal theta-naught times sine of omega t plus delta. Here the amplitude theta-naught is given as pi over ten radians. <<WRITE_STEP:theta = theta-naught sin(omega t + delta), theta-naught = pi/10 rad|id=ex-step-1-1>> Because the equation is identical to the spring's, the angle traces out a sine wave in time swinging between plus and minus its maximum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\theta = \theta_0 \sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-3|boxed>> Next we find the angular frequency. Omega equals two pi divided by the period, that is two pi over zero point zero five seconds, which gives forty pi per second. So now theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus delta. <<WRITE_STEP:omega = 2*pi / T = 2*pi / 0.05 = 40*pi per second|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we use the starting condition to find the phase constant delta. At time zero the displacement is pi over ten radians. Putting time equal to zero, pi over ten equals pi over ten times sine of delta. This gives sine of delta equals one, so delta equals pi over two. <<WRITE_STEP:At t=0: pi/10 = (pi/10) sin(delta) => sin(delta) = 1 => delta = pi/2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Substituting delta equals pi over two, theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus pi over two, which simplifies to a cosine. So the final equation is theta equals pi over ten radians times cosine of forty pi times t. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = (pi/10 rad) cos(40*pi t)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Divide torque by moment of inertia I to get angular acceleration|id=step-1>>Divide that torque by the body's moment of inertia, its resistance to being spun, and you get the angular acceleration. <<FOCUS:twisted-line>> And out pops the very same equation as the spring, just with theta in place of x and moment of inertia in place of mass, so the body swings as a smooth sine wave in time. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_8:pendulum_forces>> Why does a pendulum take exactly the same time to swing whether you pull it back a little or a lot? <<PAUSE:long>> Here is our pendulum: <<FOCUS:bob>> a heavy little ball on a light string, <<FOCUS:pivot>> fixed at the top at point O. <<SECTION:The Simple Pendulum|id=sec-1>> When the string hangs straight down, that is the resting position, where <<FOCUS:equilibrium-line>> the angle theta is zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta equals zero is rest|id=text-1>> Pull the ball aside <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> to some angle theta and let go, and it swings back and forth along a curved arc. Only two forces act on the ball: <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> its weight pulling straight down, and <<FOCUS:tension-vector>> the tension in the string. Now here is the clever part: the tension points exactly along the string, straight back to the pivot, so it can never twist the ball around that pivot. <<UNFOCUS>> It creates no turning effect at all. That leaves the weight alone to do the work. We split it: one part pulls along the string, and one part <<FOCUS:restoring-component>> pulls along the arc, back toward the resting position. That part along the arc is the restoring pull, and its size is <<FOCUS:restoring-label>> the weight times the sine of theta. <<UNFOCUS>> The further you swing out, the stronger it tugs you back. <<WRITE_TEXT:restoring force along arc grows with sine theta|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> The turning effect of the weight about the pivot equals the weight, m g, times the length of the string, times the sine of the angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = mgl\sin\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> But sine of theta is messy. So is this really simple harmonic motion, where the restoring pull must be proportional to the angle itself? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the secret: when the angle is small, the sine of theta is almost exactly equal to theta. The curve and the straight line agree. That tiny approximation is what turns a real swing into perfect simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_KEY:For small angles, sine theta is approximately theta, so the swing is simple harmonic|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Once the restoring pull is proportional to theta, the swing has a fixed rhythm, and its period depends only on the length of the string and on gravity. <<WRITE_KEY:Period depends only on length and gravity, not mass or amplitude|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> The time for one full swing equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> So a heavy ball and a light ball on the same string keep the same time, and a small pull and a big pull keep the same time. That is why a pendulum makes such a beautiful clock. <<WRITE_TEXT:same length, same time|id=text-3>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_9:physical_pendulum>> Forget the string and the little bob for a second. What if I just grabbed a metal ring, hooked it over a nail, and gave it a push? Does that swing like a pendulum too? <<PAUSE:long>> It does. And here's the big idea: <<SECTION:Physical Pendulum|id=sec-1>> any rigid body, <<FOCUS:pivot-O+body-outline>> hung from a fixed point and left to swing, is what we call a physical pendulum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Inside every object there's one special point, the centre of mass, where all its weight effectively acts. Here it is, <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass-C>> point C. When <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass-C+vertical-line>> C hangs straight down below the pivot, the body just sits there, perfectly balanced. That's the resting position, <<FOCUS:vertical-line>> where the angle is zero. Now <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> pull it aside by an angle we call theta, and <<FOCUS:line-OC>> the line from the pivot to the centre of mass tilts away from straight down. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta = angle of OC from vertical|id=text-1>> This angle theta <<FOCUS:angle-theta+vertical-line+line-OC>> between the vertical and the line to the centre of mass is the whole story. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what gravity does with it. Gravity <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> pulls the centre of mass straight down with a force m g. But notice it's pulling <<FOCUS:weight-vector+pivot-O>> off to the side of the pivot, not through it. <<UNFOCUS>> So here's the question: a force pulling to the side of a pivot, what does it create? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> A torque. A twist that tries to rotate the body back towards the resting position. <<WRITE_KEY:Restoring torque = m g l sine theta|id=key-1>> Its size is the weight m g, times <<FOCUS:line-OC>> the distance l from pivot to centre of mass, times the sine of theta. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The restoring torque equals the weight m g, times the distance l from the pivot to the centre of mass, times the sine of the angle theta, and the minus sign means it always points back towards rest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tau = -mgl\sin\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> And because it always pulls back towards zero, it's a restoring torque, exactly the ingredient we need for oscillation. The <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass-C+weight-vector>> gravity acting at the centre of mass, a distance l away, is what makes the whole rigid body swing. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A uniform rod of length one point zero zero meters is suspended through one end and set into small amplitude oscillation under gravity. We want to find the time period of oscillation. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Rod of length 1.00 m, suspended at one end, oscillates with small amplitude. Find the time period.|id=ex-q-1>> For small angles, sine theta is almost exactly theta, so the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration equals minus m g l times theta, which is the signature of simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = -mgl\sin\theta \approx -mgl\,\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> For a small amplitude the angular motion is nearly simple harmonic, so we use the physical pendulum formula: T equals two pi times the square root of I over m g l. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgl}}|id=ex-eq-1>> The period equals two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia I divided by m g l. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgl}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Now we plug in the pieces. The moment of inertia of a rod about an end is m times L squared over three, and the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass is L over two. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√[ (mL²/3) / (mg · L/2) ]|id=ex-step-1-1>> The mass m cancels top and bottom, and one factor of L cancels too, leaving T equals two pi times the square root of two L over three g. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√(2L / 3g)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substitute L equals one point zero zero meters and gravity equals nine point eight zero meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√[ (2 × 1.00) / (3 × 9.80) ]|id=ex-step-1-3>> Working that out gives the time period. And the answer is one point six four seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 1.64 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> <<SET_PARAM:theta|value=8.0>> Now there's a wrinkle. The torque depends on sine theta, not theta itself, so strictly this isn't simple harmonic motion. But for small swings, sine theta is almost exactly theta, and the motion becomes beautifully simple. <<WRITE_KEY:T = 2 pi sqrt(I / m g l)|id=key-2>> When the dust settles, the period comes out as two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia I, divided by m g l. That single formula governs any rigid body you care to hang up and swing. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_10:torsional_pendulum>> Twist a disc hanging from a thin wire, let go, and watch what happens. It doesn't just snap back to rest. It overshoots, twists the other way, and keeps going back and forth. <<SECTION:Torsional Pendulum|id=sec-1>> Here is the setup. <<FOCUS:disc+wire>> A flat disc hangs from a light wire. The top of the wire is <<FOCUS:support>> clamped firmly to a fixed support, and the wire stays perfectly vertical the whole time. Now instead of swinging it sideways like an ordinary pendulum, we rotate the disc about <<FOCUS:axis>> the wire itself as the axis. <<UNFOCUS>> The bottom of the wire turns with the disc, but the top is held fixed. <<WRITE_TEXT:Wire winds up like a twisted band|id=text-1>> So <<FOCUS:wire>> a twist builds up inside the wire, like winding up a rubber band. We rotate the disc <<FOCUS:twist-angle>> through an angle we call theta. <<UNFOCUS>> And here is the heart of it. The wire hates being twisted. It pushes back, trying to untwist itself and bring the disc home. That push-back <<FOCUS:restoring-torque>> is a restoring torque. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now I want you to predict something. If I twist the disc twice as far, how much harder does the wire push back? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Exactly twice as hard. The restoring torque is <<FOCUS:restoring-torque+twist-angle>> directly proportional to the angle of twist. <<UNFOCUS>> Double the twist, double the push-back. That single fact is what makes this motion a clock. <<PAUSE:short>> The torque equals minus the torsional constant times the angle of twist, always pointing back toward zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tau = -k\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Restoring torque tau equals minus k theta|id=key-1>> We write this as: torque equals minus k times theta. The minus sign means it always points back toward zero twist, and k is the torsional constant, a measure of how stiff the wire is. <<PAUSE:short>> Compare this to a stretched spring, where the pull is minus k times the stretch. This is the rotational twin: a restoring effect proportional to displacement. That is the exact signature of simple harmonic motion. <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>> Newton's second law for rotation says torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Substituting our restoring torque gives an angular acceleration always pointing back to centre and proportional to the angle. The angular acceleration is minus k over I times the angle, always pointing back to centre. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\alpha = -\frac{k}{I}\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:Angular acceleration equals minus k over I times theta|id=step-1>> That means the angular frequency squared, omega squared, equals k divided by I. The whole oscillation is set by just two numbers. So how long is one full back-and-forth? It depends only on how stiff the wire is, k, and how hard the disc is to spin, its moment of inertia I. <<PAUSE:short>> The time period is two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{k}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:T equals two pi root I over k|id=key-2>> The time period is two pi times the square root of I over k. A heavier disc swings slower; a stiffer wire swings faster. Notice the angle of twist is nowhere in there, so the period stays the same whether you twist it a little or a lot. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_11:two_shm_vector_sum>> Suppose a single particle feels two separate springy forces at the same time, each one tugging it back and forth. What on earth does it actually do? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's the trap your brain falls into: you imagine the two motions fighting, tangling up into some hopeless mess that you'd need new physics to describe. But the answer is astonishingly simple, and it falls right out of Newton's second law. Let's just play fair and ask one force at a time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:One force at a time|id=sec-1>> Pretend only the first force acts. By itself it gives the particle some position; call that position r one. Now pretend instead that only the second force acts. By itself it would put the particle at a different position; call that r two. Newton's second law for each force on its own says mass times the acceleration of that position equals that single force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2 r_1}{dt^2} = F_1, \qquad m\frac{d^2 r_2}{dt^2} = F_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> So if I solve each motion on its own, where does the particle really go when both forces act together at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Actual position r equals r1 plus r2, as vectors|id=key-1>> Watch. The real position is simply r one plus r two, tip to tail, the vector sum. Nothing fights, nothing tangles. <<PAUSE:short>> Why is nature this kind to us? Because Newton's second law adds. The mass times acceleration from the first equation, plus the same from the second, must equal the total force. <<PAUSE:short>> And when you add those two equations, the left side becomes the acceleration of r one plus r two, while the right side becomes the resultant force. segments.narration_chapter: Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still. Up to now we pretended a swing keeps the same size forever, swinging back and forth with a steady amplitude, driven only by a restoring force pulling it toward the center. <<SECTION:The damping force|id=sec-1>> But the real world has a second force, a brake, and we call it the damping force. Friction, air resistance, anything that resists motion. Here is its defining habit: the damping force always points opposite to the velocity. Whichever way the object moves, this force pushes back against it. <<PAUSE:short>> The braking force points opposite to the velocity, and for many real cases its size is just proportional to how fast the thing is moving. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{damp}} = -bv|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:damping force opposes velocity|id=text-1>> And in many real situations its strength is simply proportional to the speed, so we write the damping force as minus b times v. Now, a force that always opposes the velocity does negative work on the object every single moment of the motion. Negative work means it steadily removes energy. <<PAUSE:short>> So here is the honest question: if energy keeps leaking out swing after swing, what happens to the size of the swing over time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_12:damped_oscillation_curve>> Each swing carries a little less energy than the last, so each swing reaches a little less far. <<FOCUS:oscillation-curve>> The amplitude shrinks, swing after swing, until the motion dies. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The decaying envelope|id=sec-2>> <<FOCUS:first-peak>> Watch the peaks. They sit inside <<FOCUS:envelope-upper+envelope-lower>> two smooth curves that close in toward the center line, an envelope that squeezes the motion down to nothing. The motion is <<FOCUS:oscillation-curve>> still a sine wave, but its amplitude is no longer fixed; it's multiplied by a shrinking exponential that fades the swing away. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A_0\, e^{-\frac{bt}{2m}} \sin(\omega t + \phi)|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:amplitude decays inside a shrinking exponential envelope|id=key-1>> <<FOCUS:first-peak>> The first swing is the tallest, and from there every peak <<TRACE:envelope-upper>> hides beneath a fading exponential curve, all the way down to rest. <<UNFOCUS>> But notice the rhythm between the peaks barely changes. For light damping the system still oscillates with almost its natural frequency, the same frequency it would have with no brake at all. <<PAUSE:short>> So a damped oscillation is two ideas in one picture: the familiar back-and-forth rhythm, riding inside an amplitude that quietly fades to zero, <<FOCUS:rest-point>> right here at the resting point.

segments.narration_chapter: Soldiers marching in perfect step are ordered to break stride before crossing a bridge. Why would an army be afraid of walking in time? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer is hiding in a single idea: what happens when you keep pushing on something that already likes to swing back and forth. Think of a child on a swing. Left alone after one push, friction and air slowly drain the energy and the swing dies down. <<WRITE_TEXT:Free swing decays to rest|id=text-1>> But now you stand behind and give a gentle push, again and again, on your own rhythm. That repeating outside push is what we call a driving force, and the motion it creates is forced oscillation. <<SECTION:Forced oscillation|id=sec-1>> Here is the surprising part. The swing has its own favourite rhythm, its natural frequency. But push it at a different rhythm, and after a messy moment it gives in and swings at your rhythm, not its own. <<PAUSE:short>> The driver takes charge of the beat. The body ends up oscillating at the frequency of the force you apply. <<WRITE_KEY:Driven body oscillates at the driving frequency, not its natural one|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> And because every push tops up the energy that damping steals away, the swinging no longer dies out. It settles to a steady, constant size. The body feels three things at once: the spring pulling it back, the damping dragging it down, and the outside push that rises and falls with time. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{dv}{dt} = -kx - bv + F_0\sin(\omega t)|id=eq-1|boxed>> So here is the real question: if I can push at any rhythm I like, does it matter which one I choose? Is every rhythm just as good? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_13:resonance_curve>> Watch what happens to the size of the swing as I change my pushing frequency. Here is the <<FOCUS:amplitude-axis>> amplitude plotted <<FOCUS:freq-axis>> against the driving frequency. When my pushing rhythm <<FOCUS:natural-freq-line>> matches the swing's own natural rhythm, the amplitude <<FOCUS:resonance-peak>> shoots up to a peak. <<UNFOCUS>> Pushing in time with its favourite beat pours energy in most efficiently. <<SECTION:Resonance|id=sec-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> This matching condition has a name: resonance. And now look at what damping does to the picture. <<PAUSE:short>> With heavy damping <<FOCUS:curve-heavy-damping>> the peak is low and broad. But with light damping the peak becomes a <<FOCUS:curve-light-damping>> towering, razor-sharp spike, the amplitude growing enormous near the natural frequency. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> We can put numbers on it. The steady amplitude depends on how far your driving frequency sits from the natural frequency, and on the damping. The steady amplitude is large when the driving frequency omega sits <<FOCUS:natural-freq-tick>> close to the natural frequency omega-naught, and it is held in check by the damping term underneath. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now the soldiers make sense. March in step at just the wrong rhythm and you become a driving force on the bridge. Hit its natural frequency, with little damping to save you, and the resonant swing can grow until the bridge tears itself apart. <<WRITE_KEY:Resonance: drive at the natural frequency and amplitude can become huge|id=key-2>>
