lesson_plans.title: Simple Harmonic Motion: The Pull That Always Points Home

hook.text: Why does a swing always come back? Pull it far, it rushes back hard. Pull it a little, it drifts back gently. Something is steering it home — and the further you go, the harder it pulls.

crucial_facts: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration always points back toward one fixed center, and the further you are from that center, the stronger that pull.
This single rule is captured by a equals minus omega squared times x — acceleration proportional to displacement, but in the opposite direction.

diagrams.purpose: Show a particle oscillating on a straight line about a center, with the restoring acceleration arrow flipping direction and growing with displacement.

required_elements.description: A horizontal straight line representing the path of motion, the X-axis.
A clearly marked fixed point at the middle of the line, the centre of oscillation, labelled O.
A small ball sitting on the line at some displacement x to the right of the center.
A bracket or arrow from the center to the particle showing the displacement x.
An acceleration arrow on the particle pointing back toward the center, longer when the particle is further from center.

choreography.narration: Why does a swing always come back? Pull it far, it rushes back hard. Pull it a little, it drifts back gently. Something is steering it home.

Let's strip away the swing and look at the bare idea. <<SECTION:Simple Harmonic Motion|id=sec-1>>A particle moving back and forth along one straight line, around a single fixed point we call the centre of oscillation.
Here is the particle, sitting a distance x to the right of the center. We call that distance the displacement.
Now watch the one arrow that matters. The particle's acceleration always points back toward the center, never away from it.
So here is the honest question: is that homeward pull always the same strength, no matter where the particle is?
No. The further out the particle sits, the longer that arrow grows. Double the displacement, and you double the pull back toward the center.
And the instant the particle crosses to the other side of the center, the arrow flips and points back the other way. It is forever chasing the middle.

Let's say that in plain words before any symbols. <<WRITE_TEXT:accel toward center, size grows with displacement|id=text-1>>Acceleration is proportional to how far you are from the center, and it points the opposite way to your displacement.

<<WRITE_KEY:a = minus omega-squared x|id=key-1>>Now the symbols are easy. Acceleration a equals minus omega squared times x. The minus sign is the word toward; omega squared is just a fixed positive number setting how stiff the pull is.

Here's an example from the chapter. The resultant force acting on a particle executing simple harmonic motion is four newtons when it is five centimeters away from the centre of oscillation. We need to find the spring constant. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Resultant force = 4 N at 5 cm from centre. Find the spring constant k.|id=ex-q-1>>

We start from the definition of simple harmonic motion: force equals negative k times x. <<WRITE_STEP:F = -k x|id=ex-step-1-1>> Ignoring the sign, which only tells us the force is restoring, the magnitude of the spring constant k is simply the force divided by the displacement. <<WRITE_STEP:k = F / x|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we substitute the numbers. The force is four newtons and the displacement is five centimeters. But here's the careful part: we must convert centimeters to meters. Five centimeters equals five times ten to the minus two meters. <<WRITE_STEP:k = 4 N / 5 cm = 4 N / (5 × 10^-2 m)|id=ex-step-1-3>>
Dividing four by five times ten to the minus two gives eighty. So the spring constant is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_ANSWER:k = 80 N/m|id=ex-ans-1>>

Because force equals mass times acceleration, this is the same as saying the force on the particle is minus k times x. A restoring force, always tugging it home, and that is the true definition of simple harmonic motion.
So the swing was never magic. Anything pulled back toward a center by a force that grows with distance will swing in simple harmonic motion, from a pendulum to a vibrating guitar string.

equations.explanation_in_words: Acceleration is proportional to the displacement from the center, and points in the opposite direction, back toward the center.
Since force equals mass times acceleration, the restoring force is also proportional to displacement and directed back toward the center.

lesson_plans.title: The Qualitative Nature of Simple Harmonic Motion

hook.text: Why does a block on a spring keep overshooting the very place it's trying to get back to?

crucial_facts: The spring force always pushes the block back toward the center, and it grows stronger the further the block is from center: F equals minus k times x.
The block overshoots the center because at the center it is moving fastest, not slowest.

diagrams.purpose: Show the block on a frictionless table attached to a wall by a spring, with the rest point O, the pulled-out point P, and the restoring force always pointing back toward O.

required_elements.description: A vertical wall on the left to which the spring is anchored.
A coiled horizontal spring connecting the wall to the block.
A small square block sitting on the table, attached to the free end of the spring.
A horizontal frictionless surface the block slides on.
A marked point O on the table directly under the block when the spring is at natural length.
A marked point P to the right of O where the block is pulled to, showing the stretched spring.
A marked point Q to the left of O, the same distance as P, where the block momentarily stops on the other side.
An arrow on the block representing the spring restoring force, pointing back toward O.
A bracket or labeled distance from O to the block marking the displacement x.

choreography.narration: Why does a block on a spring keep overshooting the very place it's trying to get back to?
Here's our setup: a small block on a perfectly smooth, frictionless table, tied to the wall by a spring.
<<SECTION:The center point|id=sec-1>>When the spring is at its natural length, neither stretched nor squeezed, the block just sits here, at a point we'll call O.
<<WRITE_TEXT:x = displacement from O|id=text-1>>Now grab the block and pull it to the right, out to a point P, stretching the spring. That distance from O is the displacement, x.
The stretched spring pulls back, and here is the heart of it: that pull always points back toward O, and it gets stronger the further out you go.

<<WRITE_KEY:Force always points toward O, F = -kx|id=key-1>>So at every instant the force is proportional to the displacement but pointing the opposite way. That single rule is what we call simple harmonic motion.
Let go at P, and the force drags the block toward O. With nothing slowing it, the block speeds up the whole way in.
But watch what happens right at O. The spring is back to natural length, so the force is zero, yet the block is now moving as fast as it ever will.
So if there's no force pulling it any further, why doesn't the block just stop at O?
Because it's moving fast. A moving thing keeps moving, so it sails straight through the center and now squeezes the spring on the other side.
Now the compressed spring shoves it back, slowing it down, until it stops dead at Q, exactly as far out as P was, and the whole journey reverses.

<<WRITE_KEY:Fastest at center, momentarily still at the ends|id=key-2>>That's the rhythm: fastest at the center where the force is zero, momentarily frozen at the ends where the force is strongest. The overshoot happens precisely because at O the block is moving its fastest, not its slowest.
And that endless trade between speed at the middle and pull at the edges is the qualitative signature of every simple harmonic motion you'll ever meet.

equations.explanation_in_words: The force equals the spring constant times the displacement, with a minus sign because it always points back toward the center.

lesson_plans.title: The Equation of Motion of Simple Harmonic Motion

hook.text: Pull a mass on a spring, let go, and it doesn't just snap back and stop — it overshoots, comes back, overshoots again. One tiny minus sign in the force is the whole reason it wiggles forever.

crucial_facts: The defining feature of simple harmonic motion is that acceleration equals negative omega squared times displacement — always pointing back toward the center.
The velocity is largest at the center and zero at the extremes, given by v equals omega times the square root of A squared minus x squared.

diagrams.purpose: Show the particle on the X-axis with the restoring force always pointing back to the origin, so the student sees why it oscillates.

required_elements.description: A horizontal line representing the X-axis with the origin marked at its center.
A dot at the center labelled O, the center of oscillation.
A small mass m sitting on the X-axis to the right of the origin, at displacement x.
An arrow on the particle pointing back toward the origin, labelled F equals minus k x.
A mark at the far right extreme of the motion labelled A.
A mark at the far left extreme of the motion labelled minus A.

choreography.narration: Pull a mass on a spring, let go, and it doesn't just snap back and stop — it overshoots, comes back, and overshoots again. One tiny minus sign is the reason it wiggles forever.
Here's our particle of mass m, sliding along a line we'll call the X-axis, and right at the center sits the origin, the home it keeps trying to return to.
<<SECTION:The restoring force|id=sec-1>>One special force acts on it, and watch the arrow: wherever the particle is, the force points straight back toward the center.

<<WRITE_TEXT:F = -kx, minus = points home|id=text-1>>In symbols the force equals negative k times x, where k is positive and x is the distance from home. The farther it wanders, the harder it gets pulled back — and that minus sign is the whole secret.
Now force divided by mass gives acceleration, so the acceleration equals negative k over m times x. To keep the math tidy we rename k over m as omega squared.

<<WRITE_KEY:a = -omega^2 x : the signature of SHM|id=key-1>>So acceleration equals negative omega squared times displacement. That single line is the fingerprint of every simple harmonic motion in the universe.
But here's the honest question: knowing the acceleration at every point, can we figure out how fast the particle is actually moving at each spot along the line?

We use a neat trick — acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, but with the chain rule we can rewrite it so velocity sits with position. That gives v times dv equals negative omega squared times x times dx.

<<WRITE_STEP:Sum from center (x=0) out to x|id=step-1>>Now we add up all those tiny pieces from the center, where the speed is biggest, all the way out to position x. Adding them up — integrating — gives the velocity at every single point.
The particle can only reach so far before it stops and turns around. Call that farthest distance A, the amplitude.
And the same on the other side — it swings out to minus A and no farther.

<<WRITE_KEY:v = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2)|id=key-2>>So the velocity equals omega times the square root of A squared minus x squared. At the edges, where x equals A, the speed is zero — it's turning around. At the center, where x is zero, it's flat out fastest.

So that one little minus sign in the force gives us everything: a pull that always points home, an acceleration shaped like negative omega squared x, and a velocity that peaks at the center and dies at the edges. That's simple harmonic motion, fully described.

equations.explanation_in_words: The force is always proportional to how far the particle has strayed, and it points the opposite way — back toward the center.
Dividing the force by the mass gives acceleration, and we rename k over m as omega squared to keep things clean.
Using a chain-rule trick we trade the time derivative for one in displacement, so velocity and position sit on opposite sides ready to add up.
Adding up all those tiny changes from the center out to position x gives the velocity at every point, where A is the farthest the particle ever reaches.

lesson_plans.title: The Vital Signs of an Oscillation: Amplitude and Time Period

hook.text: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers could you write down that would let someone on the other side of the world rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it?

crucial_facts: The amplitude A is the farthest the particle ever gets from the center, because the sine can only swing between minus one and plus one.
The time period T is the time for one complete oscillation, after which both position and velocity return to exactly what they were.

diagrams.purpose: Show displacement as a sine curve so amplitude reads off as the height of the swing and the time period reads off as the width of one full repeat.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled time t.
Vertical axis labelled displacement x, with center line at zero.
Smooth sine curve oscillating about the time axis, showing several full cycles.
Vertical bracket from the center line up to the crest, labelled A, marking maximum displacement.
A dot at the top of a crest where displacement equals plus A.
A dot at the bottom of a trough where displacement equals minus A.
Horizontal bracket along the time axis spanning one full cycle, labelled T.

choreography.narration: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it?
Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by the very same shape, a sine curve.
<<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>>The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and the horizontal axis is time ticking forward.
Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less.
So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, reaching the crest here and the trough here.

<<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>>That height, from the center out to the crest, is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle.
<<WRITE_TEXT:A = max displacement from center|id=text-1>>Make the swing bigger or smaller and only A changes; the shape stays a perfect sine. Amplitude is the size of the motion.
<<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>>But amplitude alone is not enough. Two pendulums can swing the same distance, yet one is lazy and slow while the other is frantic and fast.
So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number?
Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction.

<<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>>The time for that one complete oscillation is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were.

Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass two hundred grams, that's two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion. The restoring force is provided by a spring of spring constant eighty newtons per meter. We need to find the time period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 200 g, k = 80 N/m. Find the time period T.|id=ex-q-1>>
We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>>

Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Working out the square root, two hundred times ten to the minus three divided by eighty gives a square root of zero point zero five seconds. So T equals two pi times zero point zero five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π × 0.05 s|id=ex-step-1-2>>
And the answer is zero point three one seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 0.31 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. A particle executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude A along the X-axis. At time t equals zero, the position of the particle is x equals A over two, and it moves along the positive x direction. We want to find the phase constant delta, given that the equation is written as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: SHM amplitude A. At t=0, x = A/2 moving in +x direction. Find phase constant delta for x = A sin(omega t + delta).|id=ex-q-1>>

We start with the position equation, x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the position is x equals A over two. <<WRITE_STEP:x = A sin(omega t + delta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So we substitute and get A over two equals A sine delta, which means sine delta equals one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A/2 = A sin(delta)  =>  sin(delta) = 1/2|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>>

The velocity is the derivative of position, so v equals A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the velocity is A omega cosine delta, and since the particle moves in the positive x direction, this must be positive. <<WRITE_STEP:v = A*omega*cos(omega t + delta);  at t=0, v = A*omega*cos(delta) > 0|id=ex-step-1-4>>

Now compare the two candidates: cosine of pi over six is positive, equal to root three over two, while cosine of five pi over six is negative, equal to minus root three over two. Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>>
And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>>
Because the motion truly repeats, the particle must be at the same place with the same velocity at time t and again at time t plus T, which is what fixes the period.

<<WRITE_TEXT:A = how big, T = how often|id=text-2>>So there it is: amplitude tells you how big the swing is, and the time period tells you how often it repeats. Two numbers, and you can rebuild the motion.

equations.explanation_in_words: Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A.
For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity.

lesson_plans.title: Simple Harmonic Motion as a Shadow of Circular Motion

hook.text: Watch the shadow of a spinning ball on a wall. The ball goes round and round at a steady speed — but its shadow doesn't. The shadow speeds up, slows, stops, and races back. That back-and-forth shadow is simple harmonic motion.

crucial_facts: The projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter is simple harmonic motion, with x equals A cosine omega t.
The shadow moves fastest at the centre and momentarily stops at the edges, even though the particle's speed never changes.

diagrams.purpose: Show a particle moving on a circle and its perpendicular foot tracing simple harmonic motion on the X-axis, so the cosine relationship becomes visible.

required_elements.description: A circle of radius A centred at the origin O.
The centre O of the circle at the origin of the axes.
Horizontal X-axis through the centre, the diameter onto which we project.
Vertical Y-axis through the centre.
The particle P moving on the circle at radius A.
The radius line from centre O to particle P.
The angle theta equals omega t between the radius OP and the X-axis.
The vertical dashed perpendicular dropped from P onto the X-axis.
The foot Q where the perpendicular meets the X-axis — the shadow of P.

choreography.narration: Watch the shadow of a spinning ball on a wall. The ball circles at a perfectly steady speed, but its shadow speeds up, slows down, stops dead, and races back the other way.
Let's build that picture exactly. Here is a particle P going around a circle of radius A at a constant rate. We call that steady spinning rate the angular speed, omega.
At the start, when time is zero, P sits on the X-axis. As time passes, the radius from the centre to P sweeps round, and the angle it makes with the X-axis is simply omega times t.
<<SECTION:The shadow on the X-axis|id=sec-1>>Now the clever move. From P, drop a straight line down onto the X-axis. The point where it lands, Q, is the particle's shadow.
As P races round the top of the circle, watch only Q. Where is Q moving fastest, and where does it momentarily stop?

At the edges, near the far left and far right, P is moving almost straight up or down, so its shadow Q barely shifts and stops for an instant. Near the centre, P moves sideways, so Q sweeps through fastest.

<<WRITE_KEY:Shadow Q is fastest at the centre, frozen at the edges|id=key-1>>That stopping at the ends and racing through the middle — that is exactly the rhythm of simple harmonic motion, even though P never changes its speed.
So how far is Q from the centre? Look at the right triangle made by the radius OP, the angle omega t, and the horizontal distance to Q.
<<WRITE_STEP:OQ is the adjacent side, OP is the hypotenuse A|id=step-1>>The distance OQ is the adjacent side, and the radius A is the hypotenuse. So OQ equals A times the cosine of the angle.
Since the angle is omega t, the position of the shadow is x equals A cosine omega t. That is the equation of simple harmonic motion, with amplitude A and angular frequency omega.
And if we drop the perpendicular onto the Y-axis instead, that shadow follows y equals A sine omega t — the very same back-and-forth, just a quarter turn out of step.

<<WRITE_KEY:Projection of circular motion onto a diameter = SHM|id=key-2>>So here is the whole idea in one line: the shadow of steady circular motion, cast onto any diameter, is simple harmonic motion. Circles and oscillations are secretly the same thing.

equations.explanation_in_words: The shadow's distance from the centre is the radius times the cosine of the angle it has turned through.
The shadow on the perpendicular axis is the radius times the sine of the same angle.

lesson_plans.title: Energy Conservation in Simple Harmonic Motion

hook.text: A mass on a spring slows to a dead stop at the edges and races fastest through the middle — yet it never loses or gains a single joule. Where does the energy hide?

crucial_facts: In simple harmonic motion, energy continuously swaps between kinetic and potential, but the total mechanical energy stays perfectly constant.
The total energy equals one half m omega squared A squared — it depends only on the amplitude, not on where the particle is right now.

diagrams.purpose: Show kinetic and potential energy trading off as the particle moves between centre and edge while the total stays fixed.

required_elements.description: A block attached to a horizontal spring, able to sit at the centre, midway, or full stretch.
A dashed vertical line marking x equals zero, the centre of oscillation.
A dashed vertical line marking x equals A, the amplitude turning point.
A vertical bar showing the magnitude of potential energy, growing as the mass moves outward.
A vertical bar showing the magnitude of kinetic energy, growing as the mass moves inward.
A vertical bar showing total energy, the same height regardless of position.

choreography.narration: A mass on a spring freezes for an instant at each edge, then whips through the middle at top speed — and yet it never loses a single joule. Where does the energy go and come back from?
<<SECTION:Potential energy in SHM|id=sec-1>>The restoring force in simple harmonic motion always pulls back toward the centre, and its strength grows the further out you go.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Work to stretch out = stored energy|id=text-1>>To drag the mass outward you have to fight that force, and the work you spend gets stored as potential energy in the spring.
Adding up that work from the centre out to a position x gives a potential energy of one half k x squared — small near the middle, largest at the very edge.
<<SECTION:Kinetic energy fills the gap|id=sec-2>>Now watch the kinetic energy: it does the exact opposite, peaking at the centre where the mass moves fastest and dropping to zero at the edges.
So at the centre it is all kinetic and no potential, and at the edge it is all potential and no kinetic — the two are forever trading places.
If one bar always rises exactly as much as the other one falls, what must happen to their sum?
<<WRITE_KEY:Total energy stays constant in SHM|id=key-1>>The sum stays flat. Every joule the potential gains, the kinetic gives up — so the total energy bar never changes height as the mass swings.
We can prove it cleanly. The position varies as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta, and the velocity as A omega cosine of omega t plus delta.

<<WRITE_STEP:Add U and K, use sin squared plus cos squared equals one|id=step-1>>Plug those into the two energies, add them, and the sine squared and cosine squared collapse to one — the time completely vanishes.

Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass forty grams, that's forty times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude two point zero centimeters, which is two point zero times ten to the minus two meters. The time period is zero point two zero seconds, and we want the total mechanical energy of the system. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 40 g, A = 2.0 cm, T = 0.20 s. Find total mechanical energy E.|id=ex-q-1>>
We start from the total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator, E equals one half m omega squared A squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now, omega equals two pi over T, so we substitute that in. The one half and the square of two pi combine to give two pi squared, and the T squared moves to the denominator, so E equals two pi squared m A squared over T squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = (1/2) m (2 pi / T)^2 A^2 = 2 pi^2 m A^2 / T^2|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Plugging in the numbers, that's two pi squared times forty times ten to the minus three kilograms, times two point zero times ten to the minus two meters squared, all divided by zero point two zero seconds squared. <<WRITE_STEP:E = 2 pi^2 (40 x 10^-3 kg)(2.0 x 10^-2 m)^2 / (0.20 s)^2|id=ex-step-1-3>>
Working that out, the total mechanical energy of the system is seven point nine times ten to the minus three joules. <<WRITE_ANSWER:E = 7.9 x 10^-3 J|id=ex-ans-1>>
<<WRITE_KEY:E = one half m omega squared A squared|id=key-2>>What is left is one half m omega squared A squared. The total energy depends only on the amplitude, never on the instant you look.
So the spring is just a perfect accountant: it shuffles energy between motion and stretch endlessly, but the books always balance to the same total.

equations.explanation_in_words: The potential energy stored at displacement x is one half k x squared, which we can also write as one half m omega squared x squared.
Adding the kinetic and potential energies, everything time-dependent cancels and the total energy is just one half m omega squared A squared.

lesson_plans.title: Angular Simple Harmonic Motion

hook.text: Push a hanging umbrella gently to one side, let go, and watch it twist back and forth — over and over, like a clock that can't make up its mind.

crucial_facts: In angular simple harmonic motion the restoring torque is proportional to the angle and always points back toward the rest position: torque equals minus k times theta.
The whole story of the straight-line spring carries over to twisting — just swap displacement x for angle theta and mass for moment of inertia.

diagrams.purpose: Show the body twisted away from its rest angle and the restoring torque that pulls it back, making the proportional-and-opposing nature of the torque visible.

required_elements.description: The vertical fixed axis the body hangs from and rotates about.
A faint dashed line marking the mean position where the angle theta is zero and the torque is zero.
A solid line representing the body rotated away from rest by an angle theta.
An arc between the rest line and the twisted line, labelled theta, showing the angular displacement.
A curved arrow pointing from the twisted position back toward the rest line, representing the restoring torque.

choreography.narration: Push a hanging umbrella gently to one side, let go, and watch it twist back and forth, over and over, like a clock that can't make up its mind.
<<SECTION:Angular SHM|id=sec-1>>It isn't sliding along a line like a block on a spring; it's rotating about a fixed axis, swinging through angles instead of distances.
There's one special angle where the body just sits still if you leave it there, the rest position, and we call that angle zero.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Rest position: net torque = 0|id=text-1>>At that rest position the total twisting force, the torque, is exactly zero, so nothing makes it turn.
Now turn it away from rest by some angle theta, and watch what wakes up.
Here is the angle theta, measuring how far we twisted the body from its resting line.
So if we twist it, what does the body actually do when we let go?
A torque appears that fights the twist, pulling the body back toward rest, and the further you turn it, the harder that torque pulls.

<<WRITE_KEY:Torque = -k theta (always pulls back to rest)|id=key-1>>That restoring torque is proportional to the angle and always points back home, and that single rule is what makes the motion angular simple harmonic.
Look closely: this is exactly the spring story, but where the spring pulled along a line, here the torque pulls around an angle.

Here's an example from the chapter. A body makes angular simple harmonic motion with amplitude theta-naught equal to pi over ten radians, and a time period of zero point zero five seconds. At time zero, the body is at a displacement theta equal to pi over ten radians. We want to write the equation giving the angular displacement as a function of time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Angular SHM, amplitude = pi/10 rad, period = 0.05 s, theta = pi/10 rad at t = 0. Find theta(t).|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by assuming the general form of the equation. Let theta equal theta-naught times sine of omega t plus delta. Here the amplitude theta-naught is given as pi over ten radians. <<WRITE_STEP:theta = theta-naught sin(omega t + delta), theta-naught = pi/10 rad|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Next we find the angular frequency. Omega equals two pi divided by the period, that is two pi over zero point zero five seconds, which gives forty pi per second. So now theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus delta. <<WRITE_STEP:omega = 2*pi / T = 2*pi / 0.05 = 40*pi per second|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we use the starting condition to find the phase constant delta. At time zero the displacement is pi over ten radians. Putting time equal to zero, pi over ten equals pi over ten times sine of delta. This gives sine of delta equals one, so delta equals pi over two. <<WRITE_STEP:At t=0: pi/10 = (pi/10) sin(delta) => sin(delta) = 1 => delta = pi/2|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Substituting delta equals pi over two, theta equals pi over ten radians times sine of forty pi t plus pi over two, which simplifies to a cosine. So the final equation is theta equals pi over ten radians times cosine of forty pi times t. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = (pi/10 rad) cos(40*pi t)|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_STEP:Divide torque by moment of inertia I to get angular acceleration|id=step-1>>Divide that torque by the body's moment of inertia, its resistance to being spun, and you get the angular acceleration.
And out pops the very same equation as the spring, just with theta in place of x and moment of inertia in place of mass, so the body swings as a smooth sine wave in time.

equations.explanation_in_words: The restoring torque equals a stiffness constant times the angle, with a minus sign because it always points back toward rest.
The angular acceleration is just the torque divided by the moment of inertia, which gives the same shape as the spring equation with omega squared standing in for k over I.
Because the equation is identical to the spring's, the angle traces out a sine wave in time swinging between plus and minus its maximum.

lesson_plans.title: The Simple Pendulum: Why It Keeps Perfect Time

hook.text: Why does a pendulum take exactly the same time to swing whether you pull it back a little or a lot?

crucial_facts: The restoring torque on a pendulum is proportional to sine theta, but for small angles sine theta is approximately theta, which is what makes the swing simple harmonic.
The time period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length and gravity, never on the mass or how far you pull it.

diagrams.purpose: Show the pendulum at an angle with weight and tension, so the student can see which force creates the restoring torque and why tension does not.

required_elements.description: The fixed support point O at the top from which the string hangs.
The light inextensible string of length l from pivot to bob.
The heavy ball (particle of mass m) at the end of the string.
Dashed vertical line straight down from pivot marking the rest position, theta equals zero.
The angle theta between the string and the vertical equilibrium line.
Arrow from the bob pointing straight down, labelled mg, the weight.
Arrow from the bob pointing back along the string toward the pivot, labelled T, the tension.
Arrow showing the component of weight along the arc, tangent to the swing, pulling the bob back toward equilibrium.

choreography.narration: Why does a pendulum take exactly the same time to swing whether you pull it back a little or a lot?
Here is our pendulum: a heavy little ball on a light string, fixed at the top at point O. <<SECTION:The Simple Pendulum|id=sec-1>>
When the string hangs straight down, that is the resting position, where the angle theta is zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta equals zero is rest|id=text-1>>
Pull the ball aside to some angle theta and let go, and it swings back and forth along a curved arc.
Only two forces act on the ball: its weight pulling straight down, and the tension in the string.
Now here is the clever part: the tension points exactly along the string, straight back to the pivot, so it can never twist the ball around that pivot. It creates no turning effect at all.
That leaves the weight alone to do the work. We split it: one part pulls along the string, and one part pulls along the arc, back toward the resting position.

That part along the arc is the restoring pull, and its size is the weight times the sine of theta. The further you swing out, the stronger it tugs you back. <<WRITE_TEXT:restoring force along arc grows with sine theta|id=text-2>>
But sine of theta is messy. So is this really simple harmonic motion, where the restoring pull must be proportional to the angle itself?

Here is the secret: when the angle is small, the sine of theta is almost exactly equal to theta. The curve and the straight line agree. That tiny approximation is what turns a real swing into perfect simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_KEY:For small angles, sine theta is approximately theta, so the swing is simple harmonic|id=key-1>>

Once the restoring pull is proportional to theta, the swing has a fixed rhythm, and its period depends only on the length of the string and on gravity. <<WRITE_KEY:Period depends only on length and gravity, not mass or amplitude|id=key-2>>

So a heavy ball and a light ball on the same string keep the same time, and a small pull and a big pull keep the same time. That is why a pendulum makes such a beautiful clock. <<WRITE_TEXT:same length, same time|id=text-3>>

equations.explanation_in_words: The turning effect of the weight about the pivot equals the weight, m g, times the length of the string, times the sine of the angle theta.
The time for one full swing equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity.

lesson_plans.title: The Physical Pendulum: Any Rigid Body Can Swing

hook.text: Forget the string and the little bob for a second. What if I just grabbed a metal ring, hooked it over a nail, and gave it a push? Does that swing like a pendulum too?

crucial_facts: A physical pendulum is any rigid body swinging about a fixed pivot, and for small swings it moves in simple harmonic motion with period two pi times the square root of I over m g l.
The restoring effect comes from gravity acting at the centre of mass, a distance l from the pivot, producing a torque of magnitude m g l sine theta.

diagrams.purpose: Show a rigid body pivoted at O, its centre of mass C at distance l, displaced by angle theta, so the restoring torque from gravity is visible.

required_elements.description: The fixed suspension point O at the top, where the body hangs from a nail or hole.
The centre of mass C of the rigid body, marked with a dot, sitting a distance l below and to the side of O.
The straight line from pivot O to centre of mass C, length l, making angle theta with the vertical.
A dashed vertical reference line straight down from O, marking the resting position theta equals zero.
The angle theta between the vertical reference line and the line OC.
The weight m g drawn as a downward arrow acting at the centre of mass C.
The outline of an irregular rigid body (e.g. a flat plate or rod) suspended at O.

choreography.narration: Forget the string and the little bob for a second. What if I just grabbed a metal ring, hooked it over a nail, and gave it a push? Does that swing like a pendulum too?
It does. And here's the big idea: <<SECTION:Physical Pendulum|id=sec-1>>any rigid body, hung from a fixed point and left to swing, is what we call a physical pendulum.
Inside every object there's one special point, the centre of mass, where all its weight effectively acts. Here it is, point C.
When C hangs straight down below the pivot, the body just sits there, perfectly balanced. That's the resting position, where the angle is zero.
Now pull it aside by an angle we call theta, and the line from the pivot to the centre of mass tilts away from straight down.
<<WRITE_TEXT:theta = angle of OC from vertical|id=text-1>>This angle theta between the vertical and the line to the centre of mass is the whole story. Watch what gravity does with it.
Gravity pulls the centre of mass straight down with a force m g. But notice it's pulling off to the side of the pivot, not through it.
So here's the question: a force pulling to the side of a pivot, what does it create?

A torque. A twist that tries to rotate the body back towards the resting position. <<WRITE_KEY:Restoring torque = m g l sine theta|id=key-1>>Its size is the weight m g, times the distance l from pivot to centre of mass, times the sine of theta.

And because it always pulls back towards zero, it's a restoring torque, exactly the ingredient we need for oscillation. The gravity acting at the centre of mass, a distance l away, is what makes the whole rigid body swing.

Here's an example from the chapter. A uniform rod of length one point zero zero meters is suspended through one end and set into small amplitude oscillation under gravity. We want to find the time period of oscillation. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Rod of length 1.00 m, suspended at one end, oscillates with small amplitude. Find the time period.|id=ex-q-1>>

For a small amplitude the angular motion is nearly simple harmonic, so we use the physical pendulum formula: T equals two pi times the square root of I over m g l. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mgl}}|id=ex-eq-1>>

Now we plug in the pieces. The moment of inertia of a rod about an end is m times L squared over three, and the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass is L over two. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√[ (mL²/3) / (mg · L/2) ]|id=ex-step-1-1>>
The mass m cancels top and bottom, and one factor of L cancels too, leaving T equals two pi times the square root of two L over three g. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√(2L / 3g)|id=ex-step-1-2>>
Substitute L equals one point zero zero meters and gravity equals nine point eight zero meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π√[ (2 × 1.00) / (3 × 9.80) ]|id=ex-step-1-3>>
Working that out gives the time period. And the answer is one point six four seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 1.64 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>>

Now there's a wrinkle. The torque depends on sine theta, not theta itself, so strictly this isn't simple harmonic motion. But for small swings, sine theta is almost exactly theta, and the motion becomes beautifully simple.

<<WRITE_KEY:T = 2 pi sqrt(I / m g l)|id=key-2>>When the dust settles, the period comes out as two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia I, divided by m g l. That single formula governs any rigid body you care to hang up and swing.

equations.explanation_in_words: The restoring torque equals the weight m g, times the distance l from the pivot to the centre of mass, times the sine of the angle theta, and the minus sign means it always points back towards rest.
For small angles, sine theta is almost exactly theta, so the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration equals minus m g l times theta, which is the signature of simple harmonic motion.
The period equals two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia I divided by m g l.

lesson_plans.title: The Torsional Pendulum: Time Kept by a Twist

hook.text: Twist a disc hanging from a wire, let go, and it doesn't just snap back — it overshoots, twists the other way, and keeps oscillating. The wire has become a clock.

crucial_facts: The twisted wire pushes back with a torque proportional to the angle of twist: tau equals minus k theta, which is exactly what makes the motion simple harmonic.
The time period depends only on the wire's stiffness k and the disc's moment of inertia I: T equals two pi times the square root of I over k.

diagrams.purpose: Show the disc suspended by a wire, the twist angle, and the restoring torque that drives the oscillation.

required_elements.description: A fixed horizontal support at the top from which the wire hangs, with hatching to show it is clamped.
A thin vertical wire running from the support down to the centre of the disc.
A flat horizontal disc suspended at the bottom of the wire, viewed slightly from above so rotation is visible.
A curved arrow at the disc showing the angle theta the disc has been rotated through about the vertical wire axis.
A curved arrow opposite to the twist showing the restoring torque the wire exerts back on the disc.
A dashed vertical line through the wire marking the axis of rotation.

choreography.narration: Twist a disc hanging from a thin wire, let go, and watch what happens. It doesn't just snap back to rest. It overshoots, twists the other way, and keeps going back and forth.

<<SECTION:Torsional Pendulum|id=sec-1>>Here is the setup. A flat disc hangs from a light wire. The top of the wire is clamped firmly to a fixed support, and the wire stays perfectly vertical the whole time.
Now instead of swinging it sideways like an ordinary pendulum, we rotate the disc about the wire itself as the axis. The bottom of the wire turns with the disc, but the top is held fixed.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Wire winds up like a twisted band|id=text-1>>So a twist builds up inside the wire, like winding up a rubber band. We rotate the disc through an angle we call theta.
And here is the heart of it. The wire hates being twisted. It pushes back, trying to untwist itself and bring the disc home. That push-back is a restoring torque.
Now I want you to predict something. If I twist the disc twice as far, how much harder does the wire push back?
Exactly twice as hard. The restoring torque is directly proportional to the angle of twist. Double the twist, double the push-back. That single fact is what makes this motion a clock.

<<WRITE_KEY:Restoring torque tau equals minus k theta|id=key-1>>We write this as: torque equals minus k times theta. The minus sign means it always points back toward zero twist, and k is the torsional constant, a measure of how stiff the wire is.

Compare this to a stretched spring, where the pull is minus k times the stretch. This is the rotational twin: a restoring effect proportional to displacement. That is the exact signature of simple harmonic motion.

<<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>>Newton's second law for rotation says torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Substituting our restoring torque gives an angular acceleration always pointing back to centre and proportional to the angle.

<<WRITE_STEP:Angular acceleration equals minus k over I times theta|id=step-1>>That means the angular frequency squared, omega squared, equals k divided by I. The whole oscillation is set by just two numbers.
So how long is one full back-and-forth? It depends only on how stiff the wire is, k, and how hard the disc is to spin, its moment of inertia I.

<<WRITE_KEY:T equals two pi root I over k|id=key-2>>The time period is two pi times the square root of I over k. A heavier disc swings slower; a stiffer wire swings faster. Notice the angle of twist is nowhere in there, so the period stays the same whether you twist it a little or a lot.

equations.explanation_in_words: The torque equals minus the torsional constant times the angle of twist, always pointing back toward zero.
The angular acceleration is minus k over I times the angle, always pointing back to centre.
The time period is two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional constant.

lesson_plans.title: Two Pushes at Once: The Superposition of Simple Harmonic Motions

hook.text: Suppose a single particle feels two separate springy forces at the same time, each one tugging it back and forth. What on earth does it actually do?

crucial_facts: When two forces act together, the particle's position is just the vector sum of where each force alone would have placed it.
Because Newton's second law is linear, you can solve each simple harmonic motion separately and simply add the answers.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the true position r is the vector sum of r1 (from force one alone) and r2 (from force two alone).

required_elements.description: The starting point of both displacement vectors.
Position r1 the particle would have if only force one acted.
Position r2 the particle would have if only force two acted.
Actual position r when both forces act, the vector sum.
Label for r1.
Label for r2.
Label for the resultant r.

choreography.narration: Suppose a single particle feels two separate springy forces at the same time, each one tugging it back and forth. What on earth does it actually do?
Here's the trap your brain falls into: you imagine the two motions fighting, tangling up into some hopeless mess that you'd need new physics to describe.
But the answer is astonishingly simple, and it falls right out of Newton's second law. Let's just play fair and ask one force at a time.
<<SECTION:One force at a time|id=sec-1>>Pretend only the first force acts. By itself it gives the particle some position; call that position r one.
Now pretend instead that only the second force acts. By itself it would put the particle at a different position; call that r two.
So if I solve each motion on its own, where does the particle really go when both forces act together at once?
<<WRITE_KEY:Actual position r equals r1 plus r2, as vectors|id=key-1>>Watch. The real position is simply r one plus r two, tip to tail, the vector sum. Nothing fights, nothing tangles.
Why is nature this kind to us? Because Newton's second law adds. The mass times acceleration from the first equation, plus the same from the second, must equal the total force.

And when you add those two equations, the left side becomes the acceleration of r one plus r two, while the right side becomes the resultant force. So that sum r one plus r two is exactly the true motion.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Velocities add too: u equals u1 plus u2|id=text-1>>The very same trick works for velocities. The real velocity is the velocity from force one plus the velocity from force two, added as vectors.

Here's an example from the chapter. We have two simple harmonic motions along the x-axis with the same frequency. The first has an amplitude of two point zero centimeters, and the second also has an amplitude of two point zero centimeters. The phase difference between them is pi over three, which is sixty degrees. We want the amplitude of the combined motion. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Combine x1 = (2.0 cm) sin wt and x2 = (2.0 cm) sin(wt + pi/3); find resultant amplitude|id=ex-q-1>>

Since both motions are along the same direction, we combine their amplitudes using the resultant amplitude formula: A equals the square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus two times A one times A two times cosine of delta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2 A_1 A_2 \cos\delta}|id=ex-eq-1>>

Now we substitute the values. A one is two point zero centimeters, A two is two point zero centimeters, and delta is pi over three. <<WRITE_STEP:A = sqrt[(2.0 cm)^2 + (2.0 cm)^2 + 2(2.0 cm)^2 cos(pi/3)]|id=ex-step-1-1>>

The cosine of pi over three equals one half, so the last term becomes two times two point zero squared times one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A = sqrt[4.0 + 4.0 + 2(4.0)(1/2)] cm = sqrt[12.0] cm|indent=1|id=ex-step-1-2>>
Taking the square root, the resultant amplitude comes out to three point five centimeters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A = 3.5 cm|id=ex-ans-1>>
This shortcut has a famous name, the principle of superposition. Solve each simple harmonic motion in peace, then just add the answers.
So two forces at once never need new physics. The actual position is the vector sum of where each force alone would have placed it, and that is the whole secret.

equations.latex: m\frac{d^2 r_1}{dt^2} = F_1, \qquad m\frac{d^2 r_2}{dt^2} = F_2
equations.explanation_in_words: Newton's second law for each force on its own says mass times the acceleration of that position equals that single force.
Adding the two equations, the mass times the acceleration of the sum r one plus r two equals the total of both forces, which is the real resultant force.
So the actual position is the vector sum of the two separate positions, and the actual velocity is the vector sum of the two separate velocities.

lesson_plans.title: Damped Harmonic Motion: Why Every Swing Dies

hook.text: Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still. Where did all that motion go?

crucial_facts: A damping force always opposes the velocity and drains energy, so the amplitude shrinks over time.
With light damping the oscillation keeps almost its natural frequency, but the swing decays inside a fading envelope.

diagrams.purpose: Show the oscillation living inside a shrinking exponential envelope, so the student sees decay and rhythm at once.

required_elements.description: Horizontal time axis pointing right, labelled time.
Vertical displacement axis through the origin, labelled displacement x.
A sine wave whose peaks shrink steadily as time increases, oscillating about the time axis and settling toward zero.
Smooth decaying exponential curve hugging the tops of the oscillation peaks from above.
Mirror-image decaying exponential curve hugging the bottoms of the oscillation troughs.
Marker at the tall first peak of the oscillation, showing the initial amplitude.
Marker far along the time axis where the curve has flattened to zero, the resting position.

choreography.narration: Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still.
Up to now we pretended a swing keeps the same size forever, swinging back and forth with a steady amplitude, driven only by a restoring force pulling it toward the center.
<<SECTION:The damping force|id=sec-1>>But the real world has a second force, a brake, and we call it the damping force. Friction, air resistance, anything that resists motion.
Here is its defining habit: the damping force always points opposite to the velocity. Whichever way the object moves, this force pushes back against it.
<<WRITE_TEXT:damping force opposes velocity|id=text-1>>And in many real situations its strength is simply proportional to the speed, so we write the damping force as minus b times v.
Now, a force that always opposes the velocity does negative work on the object every single moment of the motion. Negative work means it steadily removes energy.
So here is the honest question: if energy keeps leaking out swing after swing, what happens to the size of the swing over time?
Each swing carries a little less energy than the last, so each swing reaches a little less far. The amplitude shrinks, swing after swing, until the motion dies.
<<SECTION:The decaying envelope|id=sec-2>>Watch the peaks. They sit inside two smooth curves that close in toward the center line, an envelope that squeezes the motion down to nothing.

<<WRITE_KEY:amplitude decays inside a shrinking exponential envelope|id=key-1>>The first swing is the tallest, and from there every peak hides beneath a fading exponential curve, all the way down to rest.
But notice the rhythm between the peaks barely changes. For light damping the system still oscillates with almost its natural frequency, the same frequency it would have with no brake at all.
So a damped oscillation is two ideas in one picture: the familiar back-and-forth rhythm, riding inside an amplitude that quietly fades to zero, right here at the resting point.

equations.explanation_in_words: The braking force points opposite to the velocity, and for many real cases its size is just proportional to how fast the thing is moving.
The motion is still a sine wave, but its amplitude is no longer fixed; it's multiplied by a shrinking exponential that fades the swing away.

lesson_plans.title: Forced Oscillation and Resonance

hook.text: Soldiers marching in perfect step are ordered to break stride before they cross a bridge. Why would an army be afraid of walking in time?

crucial_facts: When you drive an oscillator, it eventually oscillates at the frequency of the driving force, not its own natural frequency.
Resonance is when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency, and the amplitude shoots up — dramatically so when damping is small.

diagrams.purpose: Show amplitude as a function of driving frequency, with a tall peak at the natural frequency that grows sharper as damping shrinks.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled driving frequency, with a tick marked natural frequency near the middle.
Vertical axis labelled amplitude of oscillation.
A faint vertical dashed line at the natural frequency position on the frequency axis.
A low, broad hump peaking modestly at the natural frequency, representing large damping.
A tall, narrow spike peaking far higher at the natural frequency, representing small damping.
The point at the very top of the light-damping curve, sitting directly above the natural frequency line.

choreography.narration: Soldiers marching in perfect step are ordered to break stride before crossing a bridge. Why would an army be afraid of walking in time?
The answer is hiding in a single idea: what happens when you keep pushing on something that already likes to swing back and forth.
Think of a child on a swing. Left alone after one push, friction and air slowly drain the energy and the swing dies down. <<WRITE_TEXT:Free swing decays to rest|id=text-1>>

But now you stand behind and give a gentle push, again and again, on your own rhythm. That repeating outside push is what we call a driving force, and the motion it creates is forced oscillation. <<SECTION:Forced oscillation|id=sec-1>>

Here is the surprising part. The swing has its own favourite rhythm, its natural frequency. But push it at a different rhythm, and after a messy moment it gives in and swings at your rhythm, not its own.
The driver takes charge of the beat. The body ends up oscillating at the frequency of the force you apply. <<WRITE_KEY:Driven body oscillates at the driving frequency, not its natural one|id=key-1>>
And because every push tops up the energy that damping steals away, the swinging no longer dies out. It settles to a steady, constant size.
So here is the real question: if I can push at any rhythm I like, does it matter which one I choose? Is every rhythm just as good?
Watch what happens to the size of the swing as I change my pushing frequency. Here is the amplitude plotted against the driving frequency.

When my pushing rhythm matches the swing's own natural rhythm, the amplitude shoots up to a peak. Pushing in time with its favourite beat pours energy in most efficiently. <<SECTION:Resonance|id=sec-2>>
This matching condition has a name: resonance. And now look at what damping does to the picture.
With heavy damping the peak is low and broad. But with light damping the peak becomes a towering, razor-sharp spike, the amplitude growing enormous near the natural frequency.
We can put numbers on it. The steady amplitude depends on how far your driving frequency sits from the natural frequency, and on the damping.

Now the soldiers make sense. March in step at just the wrong rhythm and you become a driving force on the bridge. Hit its natural frequency, with little damping to save you, and the resonant swing can grow until the bridge tears itself apart. <<WRITE_KEY:Resonance: drive at the natural frequency and amplitude can become huge|id=key-2>>

equations.explanation_in_words: The body feels three things at once: the spring pulling it back, the damping dragging it down, and the outside push that rises and falls with time.
The steady amplitude is large when the driving frequency omega sits close to the natural frequency omega-naught, and it is held in check by the damping term underneath.

segments.raw_narration: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it?
segments.text_with_markers: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by the very same shape, a sine curve.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_4:shm_displacement_graph>> Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by the very same shape, a sine curve. <<TRACE:sine-curve>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>>The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and the horizontal axis is time ticking forward.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:displacement-axis>> <<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>>The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and the horizontal axis is time ticking forward.

segments.raw_narration: Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less.

segments.raw_narration: So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, reaching the crest here and the trough here.
segments.text_with_markers: So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, reaching the crest here and the trough here. <<POINT:crest-point>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>>That height, from the center out to the crest, is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:amplitude-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>>That height, from the center out to the crest, is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A.
segments.text_with_markers: Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:A = max displacement from center|id=text-1>>Make the swing bigger or smaller and only A changes; the shape stays a perfect sine. Amplitude is the size of the motion.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>>But amplitude alone is not enough. Two pendulums can swing the same distance, yet one is lazy and slow while the other is frantic and fast.

segments.raw_narration: So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:time-axis>> So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction. <<POINT:period-bracket>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>>The time for that one complete oscillation is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> <<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>>The time for that one complete oscillation is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity.
segments.text_with_markers: For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin(\omega t + \delta) = \sin[\omega(t + T) + \delta]|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass two hundred grams, that's two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion. The restoring force is provided by a spring of spring constant eighty newtons per meter. We need to find the time period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 200 g, k = 80 N/m. Find the time period T.|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Working out the square root, two hundred times ten to the minus three divided by eighty gives a square root of zero point zero five seconds. So T equals two pi times zero point zero five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π × 0.05 s|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: And the answer is zero point three one seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 0.31 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>>

segments.raw_narration: We start with the position equation, x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the position is x equals A over two. <<WRITE_STEP:x = A sin(omega t + delta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So we substitute and get A over two equals A sine delta, which means sine delta equals one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A/2 = A sin(delta)  =>  sin(delta) = 1/2|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>>
segments.text_with_markers: Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>>

segments.raw_narration: The velocity is the derivative of position, so v equals A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the velocity is A omega cosine delta, and since the particle moves in the positive x direction, this must be positive. <<WRITE_STEP:v = A*omega*cos(omega t + delta);  at t=0, v = A*omega*cos(delta) > 0|id=ex-step-1-4>>

segments.raw_narration: Now compare the two candidates: cosine of pi over six is positive, equal to root three over two, while cosine of five pi over six is negative, equal to minus root three over two. Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>>

Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>>

segments.raw_narration: And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>>

lesson_narrations.full_text_with_markers: A pendulum swings, a guitar string hums, a child rocks on a swing. What three numbers would let someone rebuild that exact motion without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_4:shm_displacement_graph>> Here is the secret: every one of those motions, no matter how different they look, is described by the very same shape, a sine curve. <<TRACE:sine-curve>> <<FOCUS:displacement-axis>> <<SECTION:Amplitude|id=sec-1>>The vertical axis is displacement, how far our particle is from the center, and the horizontal axis is time ticking forward. <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> Now a sine is a fussy thing: it can only ever take values between minus one and plus one, never more, never less. So if displacement is A times that sine, the particle can only ever swing between minus A and plus A, reaching the crest here and the trough here. <<POINT:crest-point>> <<FOCUS:amplitude-line>> <<WRITE_KEY:Amplitude A = farthest from center, since sine lives between minus one and plus one|id=key-1>>That height, from the center out to the crest, is the amplitude A: simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the middle. <<PAUSE:short>> Displacement equals the amplitude A multiplied by the sine of an angle that grows with time; since the sine never leaves minus one to plus one, x never leaves minus A to plus A. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A\sin(\omega t + \delta)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:trough-point>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = max displacement from center|id=text-1>>Make the swing bigger or smaller and only A changes; the shape stays a perfect sine. Amplitude is the size of the motion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> <<SECTION:Time Period|id=sec-2>>But amplitude alone is not enough. Two pendulums can swing the same distance, yet one is lazy and slow while the other is frantic and fast. <<FOCUS:time-axis>> So how do we capture the rhythm, the how-fast-it-repeats, in a single number? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> Watch one full cycle: the particle leaves a position with some velocity, wanders out and back, and returns to that exact position with that exact velocity in the same direction. <<POINT:period-bracket>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> <<WRITE_KEY:Time period T = one full oscillation; position AND velocity repeat|id=key-2>>The time for that one complete oscillation is the time period T, after which both position and velocity are back to exactly what they were. <<PAUSE:short>> For the motion to repeat, the displacement at time t must equal the displacement one period later, at time t plus T, and the same is true for the velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin(\omega t + \delta) = \sin[\omega(t + T) + \delta]|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle of mass two hundred grams, that's two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, executes simple harmonic motion. The restoring force is provided by a spring of spring constant eighty newtons per meter. We need to find the time period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: m = 200 g, k = 80 N/m. Find the time period T.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the formula for the time period of a spring oscillator: T equals two pi times the square root of mass over force constant k. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we substitute the values. The mass m is two hundred times ten to the minus three kilograms, and the spring constant k is eighty newtons per meter. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π √(200×10⁻³ kg / 80 N/m)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the square root, two hundred times ten to the minus three divided by eighty gives a square root of zero point zero five seconds. So T equals two pi times zero point zero five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:T = 2π × 0.05 s|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is zero point three one seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:T = 0.31 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A particle executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude A along the X-axis. At time t equals zero, the position of the particle is x equals A over two, and it moves along the positive x direction. We want to find the phase constant delta, given that the equation is written as x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: SHM amplitude A. At t=0, x = A/2 moving in +x direction. Find phase constant delta for x = A sin(omega t + delta).|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the position equation, x equals A sine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the position is x equals A over two. <<WRITE_STEP:x = A sin(omega t + delta)|id=ex-step-1-1>> So we substitute and get A over two equals A sine delta, which means sine delta equals one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A/2 = A sin(delta)  =>  sin(delta) = 1/2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now, sine delta equals one half gives two possible angles: delta equals pi over six, or delta equals five pi over six. To decide between them, we look at the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(delta) = 1/2  =>  delta = pi/6  or  5pi/6|id=ex-step-1-3>> The velocity is the derivative of position, so v equals A omega cosine of omega t plus delta. At time t equals zero, the velocity is A omega cosine delta, and since the particle moves in the positive x direction, this must be positive. <<WRITE_STEP:v = A*omega*cos(omega t + delta);  at t=0, v = A*omega*cos(delta) > 0|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now compare the two candidates: cosine of pi over six is positive, equal to root three over two, while cosine of five pi over six is negative, equal to minus root three over two. Since the velocity must be positive at time t equals zero, delta must equal pi over six. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(pi/6) = +sqrt(3)/2 > 0;  cos(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0|id=ex-step-1-5>> And so the phase constant is delta equals pi over six. <<WRITE_ANSWER:delta = pi/6|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:period-bracket>> Because the motion truly repeats, the particle must be at the same place with the same velocity at time t and again at time t plus T, which is what fixes the period. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sine-curve>> <<WRITE_TEXT:A = how big, T = how often|id=text-2>>So there it is: amplitude tells you how big the swing is, and the time period tells you how often it repeats. Two numbers, and you can rebuild the motion.

segments.raw_narration: A mass on a spring freezes for an instant at each edge, then whips through the middle at top speed — and yet it never loses a single joule. Where does the energy go and come back from?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:spring-mass>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_6:shm_energy_bars>> A mass on a spring freezes for an instant at each edge, then whips through the middle at top speed — and yet it never loses a single joule. Where does the energy go and come back from? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Potential energy in SHM|id=sec-1>>The restoring force in simple harmonic motion always pulls back toward the centre, and its strength grows the further out you go.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Potential energy in SHM|id=sec-1>>The restoring force in simple harmonic motion always pulls back toward the centre, and its strength grows the further out you go. <<POINT:centre-line>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Work to stretch out = stored energy|id=text-1>>To drag the mass outward you have to fight that force, and the work you spend gets stored as potential energy in the spring.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:edge-line>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Work to stretch out = stored energy|id=text-1>>To drag the mass outward you have to fight that force, and the work you spend gets stored as potential energy in the spring.

segments.raw_narration: Adding up that work from the centre out to a position x gives a potential energy of one half k x squared — small near the middle, largest at the very edge.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:pe-bar>> Adding up that work from the centre out to a position x gives a potential energy of one half k x squared — small near the middle, largest at the very edge.

segments.raw_narration: The potential energy stored at displacement x is one half k x squared, which we can also write as one half m omega squared x squared.
segments.text_with_markers: The potential energy stored at displacement x is one half k x squared, which we can also write as one half m omega squared x squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:U(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} m \omega^2 x^2|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Kinetic energy fills the gap|id=sec-2>>Now watch the kinetic energy: it does the exact opposite, peaking at the centre where the mass moves fastest and dropping to zero at the edges.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:ke-bar>> <<SECTION:Kinetic energy fills the gap|id=sec-2>>Now watch the kinetic energy: it does the exact opposite, peaking at the centre where the mass moves fastest and dropping to zero at the edges.

segments.raw_narration: So at the centre it is all kinetic and no potential, and at the edge it is all potential and no kinetic — the two are forever trading places.
segments.text_with_markers: So at the centre it is all kinetic and no potential, and at the edge it is all potential and no kinetic — the two are forever trading places. <<POINT:spring-mass>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Why does a pendulum take exactly the same time to swing whether you pull it back a little or a lot?
