segments.raw_narration: Here is our pendulum: a heavy little ball on a light string, fixed at the top at point O. <<SECTION:The Simple Pendulum|id=sec-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:string>> Here is our pendulum: a heavy little ball on a light string, fixed at the top at point O. <<SECTION:The Simple Pendulum|id=sec-1>> <<TRACE:string>>

segments.raw_narration: When the string hangs straight down, that is the resting position, where the angle theta is zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta equals zero is rest|id=text-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:equilibrium-line>> When the string hangs straight down, that is the resting position, where the angle theta is zero. <<WRITE_TEXT:theta equals zero is rest|id=text-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Pull the ball aside to some angle theta and let go, and it swings back and forth along a curved arc.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> Pull the ball aside to some angle theta and let go, and it swings back and forth along a curved arc.

segments.raw_narration: Only two forces act on the ball: its weight pulling straight down, and the tension in the string.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> Only two forces act on the ball: its weight pulling straight down, and the tension in the string. <<POINT:weight-vector>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the clever part: the tension points exactly along the string, straight back to the pivot, so it can never twist the ball around that pivot. It creates no turning effect at all.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:tension-vector>> Now here is the clever part: the tension points exactly along the string, straight back to the pivot, so it can never twist the ball around that pivot. It creates no turning effect at all. <<POINT:tension-vector>>

segments.raw_narration: That leaves the weight alone to do the work. We split it: one part pulls along the string, and one part pulls along the arc, back toward the resting position.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:restoring-component>> That leaves the weight alone to do the work. We split it: one part pulls along the string, and one part pulls along the arc, back toward the resting position. <<TRACE:restoring-component>>

segments.raw_narration: That part along the arc is the restoring pull, and its size is the weight times the sine of theta. The further you swing out, the stronger it tugs you back. <<WRITE_TEXT:restoring force along arc grows with sine theta|id=text-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:restoring-component>> That part along the arc is the restoring pull, and its size is the weight times the sine of theta. The further you swing out, the stronger it tugs you back. <<WRITE_TEXT:restoring force along arc grows with sine theta|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The turning effect of the weight about the pivot equals the weight, m g, times the length of the string, times the sine of the angle theta.
segments.text_with_markers: The turning effect of the weight about the pivot equals the weight, m g, times the length of the string, times the sine of the angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = mgl\sin\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: But sine of theta is messy. So is this really simple harmonic motion, where the restoring pull must be proportional to the angle itself?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> But sine of theta is messy. So is this really simple harmonic motion, where the restoring pull must be proportional to the angle itself? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Here is the secret: when the angle is small, the sine of theta is almost exactly equal to theta. The curve and the straight line agree. That tiny approximation is what turns a real swing into perfect simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_KEY:For small angles, sine theta is approximately theta, so the swing is simple harmonic|id=key-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> Here is the secret: when the angle is small, the sine of theta is almost exactly equal to theta. The curve and the straight line agree. That tiny approximation is what turns a real swing into perfect simple harmonic motion. <<WRITE_KEY:For small angles, sine theta is approximately theta, so the swing is simple harmonic|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Once the restoring pull is proportional to theta, the swing has a fixed rhythm, and its period depends only on the length of the string and on gravity. <<WRITE_KEY:Period depends only on length and gravity, not mass or amplitude|id=key-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:string>> Once the restoring pull is proportional to theta, the swing has a fixed rhythm, and its period depends only on the length of the string and on gravity. <<WRITE_KEY:Period depends only on length and gravity, not mass or amplitude|id=key-2>> <<TRACE:string>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The time for one full swing equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity.
segments.text_with_markers: The time for one full swing equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: So a heavy ball and a light ball on the same string keep the same time, and a small pull and a big pull keep the same time. That is why a pendulum makes such a beautiful clock. <<WRITE_TEXT:same length, same time|id=text-3>>

segments.raw_narration: Suppose a single particle feels two separate springy forces at the same time, each one tugging it back and forth. What on earth does it actually do?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:origin>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_11:two_shm_vector_sum>> Suppose a single particle feels two separate springy forces at the same time, each one tugging it back and forth. What on earth does it actually do? <<POINT:origin>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's the trap your brain falls into: you imagine the two motions fighting, tangling up into some hopeless mess that you'd need new physics to describe.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:origin>> Here's the trap your brain falls into: you imagine the two motions fighting, tangling up into some hopeless mess that you'd need new physics to describe.

segments.raw_narration: But the answer is astonishingly simple, and it falls right out of Newton's second law. Let's just play fair and ask one force at a time.
segments.text_with_markers: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:origin>> But the answer is astonishingly simple, and it falls right out of Newton's second law. Let's just play fair and ask one force at a time. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:One force at a time|id=sec-1>>Pretend only the first force acts. By itself it gives the particle some position; call that position r one.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:vector_a>> <<SECTION:One force at a time|id=sec-1>>Pretend only the first force acts. By itself it gives the particle some position; call that position r one. <<TRACE:vector_a>>

segments.raw_narration: Now pretend instead that only the second force acts. By itself it would put the particle at a different position; call that r two.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:vector_b>> Now pretend instead that only the second force acts. By itself it would put the particle at a different position; call that r two. <<TRACE:vector_b>>

segments.raw_narration: Newton's second law for each force on its own says mass times the acceleration of that position equals that single force.
segments.text_with_markers: Newton's second law for each force on its own says mass times the acceleration of that position equals that single force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2 r_1}{dt^2} = F_1, \qquad m\frac{d^2 r_2}{dt^2} = F_2|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: So if I solve each motion on its own, where does the particle really go when both forces act together at once?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:origin>> So if I solve each motion on its own, where does the particle really go when both forces act together at once? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Actual position r equals r1 plus r2, as vectors|id=key-1>>Watch. The real position is simply r one plus r two, tip to tail, the vector sum. Nothing fights, nothing tangles.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant>> <<WRITE_KEY:Actual position r equals r1 plus r2, as vectors|id=key-1>>Watch. The real position is simply r one plus r two, tip to tail, the vector sum. Nothing fights, nothing tangles. <<TRACE:resultant>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Why is nature this kind to us? Because Newton's second law adds. The mass times acceleration from the first equation, plus the same from the second, must equal the total force.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:resultant>> Why is nature this kind to us? Because Newton's second law adds. The mass times acceleration from the first equation, plus the same from the second, must equal the total force. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And when you add those two equations, the left side becomes the acceleration of r one plus r two, while the right side becomes the resultant force. So that sum r one plus r two is exactly the true motion.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:resultant>> And when you add those two equations, the left side becomes the acceleration of r one plus r two, while the right side becomes the resultant force. So that sum r one plus r two is exactly the true motion. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Adding the two equations, the mass times the acceleration of the sum r one plus r two equals the total of both forces, which is the real resultant force.
segments.text_with_markers: Adding the two equations, the mass times the acceleration of the sum r one plus r two equals the total of both forces, which is the real resultant force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}(r_1 + r_2) = F_1 + F_2|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Velocities add too: u equals u1 plus u2|id=text-1>>The very same trick works for velocities. The real velocity is the velocity from force one plus the velocity from force two, added as vectors.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Velocities add too: u equals u1 plus u2|id=text-1>>The very same trick works for velocities. The real velocity is the velocity from force one plus the velocity from force two, added as vectors. <<POINT:resultant>>

segments.raw_narration: Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still.
segments.text_with_markers: Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still.

segments.raw_narration: Now, a force that always opposes the velocity does negative work on the object every single moment of the motion. Negative work means it steadily removes energy.

12.1 SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION
When a body repeats its motion after regular time
intervals we say that it is in harmonic motion or
periodic motion. The time interval after which the
motion is repeated is called the time period. If a body
moves to and fro on the same path, it is said to perform
oscillations. Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a
special type of oscillation in which the particle
oscillates on a straight line, the acceleration of the
particle is always directed towards a fixed point on the
line and its magnitude is proportional to the
displacement of the particle from this point. This fixed
point is called the centre of oscillation. Taking this
point as the origin and the line of motion as the X-axis,
we can write the defining equation of a simple
harmonic motion as

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with a simple idea you've already seen in nature. When something repeats its motion over and over, after equal chunks of time, we call that periodic motion or harmonic motion. Think of a swing going back and forth, or a clock's pendulum. The time it takes to complete one full cycle and get back to where it started is called the time period. Now, if a body moves back and forth along the same path, we say it's oscillating.

Simple harmonic motion, which we'll shorten to S H M, is a very special kind of oscillation. Here's what makes it special. First, the particle moves along a straight line. Second, its acceleration always points toward one fixed point on that line. And third, the size of that acceleration is proportional to how far the particle is from that fixed point. That fixed point is called the centre of oscillation.

Let's make this concrete. We put that centre at the origin and call the line of motion our x-axis. Then the defining rule of simple harmonic motion is that acceleration equals negative omega squared times x. Here omega squared is just a positive constant. Notice the minus sign carefully. If x is positive, meaning the particle is on one side, then acceleration comes out negative, pulling it back. If x is negative, acceleration is positive, again pulling it back. So the acceleration always points home, toward the centre.

Now let's bring in force. From Newton's second law, acceleration equals force divided by mass. So our defining equation becomes force equals negative mass times omega squared times x, which we write more simply as force equals negative k times x. Here k equals mass times omega squared, and we call it the force constant or spring constant. This gives us another way to define S H M. A particle does simple harmonic motion if the total force on it points toward a fixed point and is proportional to its distance from that point.

Think about what happens at the centre. The displacement x is zero, so the force is zero. That means the centre of oscillation is also the equilibrium position, where the particle would sit at rest. A force that always pushes the particle back toward this equilibrium is called a restoring force. And because force is proportional to displacement, this restoring force is linear. That linear relationship is the heart of simple harmonic motion.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's build a clear mental picture. Imagine a small block sitting on a perfectly smooth, frictionless table. One side of the block is attached to a wall by a spring. When the spring is at its natural length, neither stretched nor squeezed, the block rests at a point we'll call O, the center. Now suppose you grab the block and pull it sideways, stretching the spring by some distance. Let's call that point P, and that distance is the amplitude, which we'll call A. Then you let go.

Here's the key idea. At any moment, the block's displacement from O equals how much the spring is stretched or compressed. And the force the spring exerts is always proportional to that displacement but pointing back toward O. We write this as force equals minus k times x, where k is the spring constant. That minus sign is everything. It means the force always pulls the block back toward the center, never away. Because of this, the motion is simple harmonic by definition.

Now watch the block move. Released from P, the spring pulls it toward O, so the block speeds up the whole way. At O, the spring is at natural length, so there's no force, but the block is now moving fast. In fact, its speed is maximum at the center. It overshoots, sliding past O to the left, which now compresses the spring. The compressed spring pushes back to the right, slowing the block down until it stops at a point Q. Then the spring pushes it back again, and the cycle repeats forever, since there's no friction.

Here's a beautiful consequence of energy conservation. At both P and Q the block is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic energy is zero, and all the energy is stored in the spring as potential energy. Since no energy is lost, the potential energy at P must equal the potential energy at Q. That forces the distance OP to equal the distance OQ. So the block swings equal distances on both sides of the center. That maximum distance on either side is what we call the amplitude.

Notice the rhythm of energy here. At the ends, all energy is potential, stored in the spring. At the center, all energy is kinetic, in the moving block. Energy sloshes back and forth between these two forms, while the total stays the same. This trade-off is the heart of simple harmonic motion, and it's what lets us calculate things like amplitude from speed, as we'll see in a moment.

That distance from O is the displacement, x. <<POINT:displacement-x>> <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> The stretched spring pulls back, and here is the heart of it: that pull always points back toward O, and it gets stronger the further out you go. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force always points toward O, F = -kx|id=key-1>>So at every instant the force is proportional to the displacement but pointing the opposite way. topics.our_understanding:
In this section we figure out exactly how a particle moves when it's doing simple harmonic motion. Here's the setup. Imagine a particle of mass m sliding along a line we'll call the X-axis. A special force acts on it: the force always equals negative k times x, where k is some positive number and x is how far the particle is from the center, the origin. That little minus sign is the whole secret. It means the force always points back toward the center. The farther the particle wanders, the harder it gets pulled home. That's what creates the back-and-forth wiggle we call simple harmonic motion.

Now, force divided by mass gives acceleration. So the acceleration equals negative k over m times x. To make the math cleaner, we give the quantity k over m a name: we call it omega squared, where omega is the square root of k over m. So acceleration becomes negative omega squared times x. That's our equation of motion.

From here we play a clever trick. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time, but we rewrite it using the chain rule as velocity times the rate of change of velocity with position. That lets us connect velocity directly to position. After integrating from the starting point, we find a beautiful result: velocity equals omega times the square root of a constant called A squared minus x squared. Here A is the amplitude, the farthest the particle ever gets from center. Notice what this tells you: when x equals A, velocity is zero. The particle stops at the very edges. And at the center, where x is zero, velocity is biggest. That matches our everyday feel for a swing.

Then we integrate once more, this time linking position to time, and out pops the famous answer: x equals A times the sine of omega t plus delta. The particle's position traces a smooth sine wave in time. The delta is just a phase constant that depends on where the particle started. Omega is the angular frequency, telling us how fast the oscillation cycles.

Finally, taking the rate of change of position with time, we get the velocity at any moment: velocity equals A times omega times the cosine of omega t plus delta. So position follows a sine curve and velocity follows a cosine curve, perfectly out of step by a quarter cycle. This pair of equations is the complete description of simple harmonic motion. Everything else in this chapter grows from these two results.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's get familiar with the words physicists use to describe simple harmonic motion. These are like the vital signs of an oscillation, and once you know them, you can describe any back-and-forth motion precisely.

First, amplitude. The displacement of our particle follows a sine pattern, and a sine can only swing between minus one and plus one. So the displacement swings between minus A and plus A. That constant A is simply the farthest the particle ever gets from the center. We call it the amplitude.

Next, the time period. A particle in this motion keeps repeating itself. If it's at some position moving with some velocity now, after a fixed time it returns to that exact position with that same velocity in the same direction. That one full repeat is a complete oscillation, and the time it takes is the time period, written as T. Both sine and cosine repeat when their angle grows by two pi. Since the smallest such jump corresponds to one period, the angle omega times T must equal two pi. So the time period equals two pi divided by omega. And because omega is the square root of k over m, the period also equals two pi times the square root of mass divided by force constant. Notice something beautiful here: heavier mass means a longer period, and a stiffer spring means a shorter, faster oscillation.

Now frequency. Frequency is just one divided by the time period. It tells you how many oscillations happen each second, measured in hertz. And omega itself is called the angular frequency.

Then there's phase, the quantity omega t plus delta. The phase tells you the exact status of the particle at any moment. If the phase is zero, the particle is crossing the mean position heading in the positive direction. If the phase is pi over two, the particle sits at its positive extreme. As time goes on the phase grows, and adding two pi brings the particle right back to the same status.

Finally, the phase constant delta. This depends on where you choose to start your stopwatch. If you start when the particle crosses the center going positive, delta is zero, and the motion is a pure sine. If you start at the positive extreme, delta is pi over two, which turns the sine into a cosine. So sine form and cosine form are really the same motion, just with different starting choices.

topics.our_understanding:
Here's a beautiful idea that ties two motions together. Imagine a particle moving around a circle of radius A at a steady speed. Not changing how fast it spins, just going round and round smoothly. We call that steady spinning rate the angular speed, omega. Now place the center of the circle at the origin, and draw two perpendicular lines through it, our X-axis and Y-axis. At the very start, when time is zero, let's say our particle sits right on the X-axis. As time goes on, the line from the center to the particle sweeps around, making an angle with the X-axis. That angle is simply omega times t, because the particle turns at a steady rate.

Now here's the clever move. From the particle, drop a straight line down onto the X-axis. The point where it lands, call it Q, is the particle's shadow on the X-axis. Its position is A times the cosine of omega t. Do the same thing onto the Y-axis, and that shadow R sits at A times the sine of omega t.

Look at what those two shadows are doing. As the particle circles around, each shadow slides back and forth along its axis. And the position A times cosine of omega t is exactly the equation of simple harmonic motion. So the shadow on the X-axis is doing perfect simple harmonic motion, with amplitude A and angular frequency omega. The shadow on the Y-axis is doing the same thing, also with amplitude A and the same angular frequency.

There's one neat difference between them. One follows a cosine, the other follows a sine. And cosine of omega t is the same as sine of omega t plus a quarter turn. So these two simple harmonic motions are out of step with each other by ninety degrees, or pi over two in radians. We say their phases differ by pi over two.

The big takeaway is this: if you take a uniform circular motion and project it onto any diameter, what you get is simple harmonic motion. This connection is wonderful because circular motion is easy to picture and easy to work with. Whenever you struggle to imagine an oscillation, just remember it's the shadow of something going steadily around a circle. That single picture explains why simple harmonic motion has the amplitude, frequency, and phase that it does.

topics.our_understanding:
In this section we look at how energy behaves during simple harmonic motion, and the beautiful result is that the total energy stays perfectly constant. Let's build it up. Remember that in simple harmonic motion, the force always points back toward the center and is given by force equals minus k times x, where x is how far the particle is from the center. Now, whenever a force acts over a small distance, it does work. If we add up the work done as the particle moves from the center out to some position x, we find the work equals minus one half k times x squared. The minus sign tells us the force fights the outward motion.

From that work we get the potential energy. The change in potential energy is the negative of the work done, so the potential energy at position x equals one half k times x squared. We choose the potential energy to be zero right at the center of the oscillation, which keeps things tidy. Since k equals m times omega squared, we can also write the potential energy as one half times m times omega squared times x squared. That's the same spring formula you've already been using.

Now think about what happens over time. The position swings as A times the sine of omega t plus delta, and the velocity swings as A times omega times the cosine of the same angle. When you plug these in, the potential energy depends on sine squared, and the kinetic energy depends on cosine squared. Here's the magic: when you add them, sine squared plus cosine squared always equals one. So the total energy becomes one half times m times omega squared times A squared, and notice there's no time left in that expression. The energy is constant.

Picture a block on a smooth surface attached to a spring. At the center, the spring is relaxed, the potential energy is zero, and all the energy is kinetic, because the block is moving fastest there. As the block moves outward, it slows down, kinetic energy shrinks while potential energy grows. At the very ends, where displacement equals plus or minus A, the block stops for an instant, so kinetic energy is zero and all the energy is now potential, reaching its maximum of one half k times A squared. Energy just keeps trading back and forth between motion and stored spring energy, but the total never changes.

Here's an example from the chapter. topics.our_understanding:
So far we've talked about things that move back and forth in a straight line, like a block on a spring. But objects can also swing back and forth by rotating, and that's what this section is about. Think about a hanging umbrella. If you push it gently to one side and let go, it twists back and forth around the axis it hangs from. That twisting oscillation is what we call angular simple harmonic motion.

For a rotation to count as angular simple harmonic motion, three things must be true. First, there must be a rest position where the total twisting force, which we call torque, is zero. That's the mean position, where the angle is zero. Second, when you turn the body away from that mean position by some angle, a torque appears that is proportional to how far you turned it. The more you twist, the stronger the restoring torque. And third, that torque always points back toward the mean position, trying to undo the twist. So the torque equals minus k times the angle, where k is a constant. The minus sign tells us it always pushes back home.

Now here's the beautiful part. In straight-line motion, force equals mass times acceleration. In rotation, torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Moment of inertia, which we write as I, is basically the rotational version of mass. When we work the math out, we get exactly the same kind of equation as we had for the block on a spring, just with angle replacing position. Because the equation has the same shape, the answer has the same shape too. The angle changes with time like a sine wave, swinging between a maximum angle on each side. We call that maximum the amplitude.

The angular frequency, written omega, is the square root of k divided by I. From that we get the time period, which is two pi times the square root of I divided by k, and the frequency is just one over the period. Notice that a larger moment of inertia, meaning a heavier or more spread-out body, makes the swing slower, while a stiffer restoring torque makes it faster.

Finally, the energy works just like before. There's potential energy stored when the body is twisted, and kinetic energy when it's moving. As it swings, energy trades back and forth between the two, but the total energy stays constant, equal to one half times I times omega squared times the amplitude squared. The system never loses energy, it just keeps passing it back and forth.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something you've probably seen your whole life without realizing it follows a beautiful rule. A simple pendulum is just a heavy little ball hanging from a light, unstretchable string fixed at the top. In real life you might use a small metal sphere on a thread, but in physics we imagine an ideal version. When the string hangs straight down, that's the resting or equilibrium position. Pull the ball to the side and let go, and it swings back and forth along a curved arc.

Now, the big question is: is this swinging simple harmonic motion? To find out, we look at the forces and the torque. Two forces act on the ball: its weight pulling straight down, and the tension in the string. The tension creates no torque about the swinging axis because it points right along the string toward the pivot. But the weight does create a torque, and that torque always tries to pull the ball back toward the center. When we work it out, this torque turns out to depend on the sine of the angle, not on the angle itself. So strictly speaking, the motion is not perfectly simple harmonic.

Here's the key trick, though. When the swing is small, the sine of an angle is very nearly equal to the angle itself, measured in radians. With that approximation, the torque becomes directly proportional to the angle, and that is exactly the condition for simple harmonic motion. So for small swings, a pendulum really does behave like a simple harmonic oscillator.

When you carry the math through, you find the time period — the time for one full back-and-forth swing — equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity. Notice what's surprising here: the mass of the ball doesn't appear at all, and neither does the size of the swing. The period depends only on the length of the string and the strength of gravity. A longer string swings more slowly; stronger gravity makes it swing faster.

We can also look at this same motion as a straight-line oscillation along the arc, and we get exactly the same period — a nice confirmation. And because the period depends on gravity, a pendulum gives us a clever way to actually measure gravity in a laboratory. You time many swings, find the period, plug into the formula rearranged for gravity, and out comes the value of g. This is one of physics' most elegant and practical ideas.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about a physical pendulum. Up to now you've probably pictured a pendulum as a little bob on a string. But here's a richer idea: take any rigid body, hang it from a fixed point, and let it swing. That's a physical pendulum. Think of a circular ring hooked over a nail, or a heavy metal rod hanging through a hole drilled near one end. Any solid object swinging about a fixed support counts.

Now imagine we hang a body through a hole at a point we'll call O. There's a special point in any object called the centre of mass, where all its weight effectively acts. When that centre of mass hangs straight down below O, the body just sits there, perfectly balanced. We call that the resting position, where the angle is zero. Pull the body to the side and let go, and it starts to oscillate, rotating back and forth about a horizontal axis through O.

What makes it swing back? Two forces act on it: its weight pulling down at the centre of mass, and the support pushing at O. The support's force acts right through O, so it produces no turning effect, no torque. But the weight does. Its torque has a size equal to the mass times gravity times the distance from the support to the centre of mass, times the sine of the angle. This torque always tries to bring the body back toward the resting position.

Here's the honest part. When you write down the angular acceleration, it comes out proportional to the sine of the angle, not the angle itself. So strictly speaking, this is not simple harmonic motion. But here's the beautiful trick: for small angles, the sine of an angle is almost exactly equal to the angle in radians. With that approximation, the angular acceleration becomes proportional to the angle, and we recover simple harmonic motion.

So for small swings, we get a clean time period. The time period equals two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the quantity mass times gravity times the distance to the centre of mass. Notice how the moment of inertia, which describes how the mass is spread out, now controls the timing. That's the key insight: a swinging rigid body keeps time based on how its mass is distributed and how far its centre of mass sits from the pivot.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's picture a torsional pendulum. Imagine you take an object, maybe a flat disc, and you hang it from a thin wire or thread attached to its center. The wire goes straight up to a fixed support. Now, instead of swinging the object side to side like a regular pendulum, you twist it. You rotate the disc around the wire as its axis, turning it through some angle. The wire stays vertical the whole time, but inside the wire a twist is created. The bottom of the wire turns with the disc, while the top stays clamped firmly to the support, so the wire gets wound up like a twisted rubber band.

Here's the key idea. When the wire is twisted, it doesn't like being twisted. It pushes back. It exerts what we call a restoring torque, trying to untwist itself and bring the disc back to where the twist is zero. And the more you twist it, the harder it pushes back. The torque is proportional to the angle of twist, which is just the angle the disc has been rotated. The number that tells us how strong this twisting resistance is, is called the torsional constant of the wire. So the restoring torque equals the torsional constant times the angle.

Now think about what that means. We have a body with some moment of inertia, and the torque trying to bring it back is proportional to how far it's turned, but in the opposite direction. That's exactly the recipe for simple harmonic motion, just in a rotational form. Notice the parallel: in a normal spring, force is proportional to displacement; here, torque is proportional to angular displacement.

Because it follows the same pattern, the motion is simple harmonic. The angular acceleration equals the negative of a constant times the angle, where that constant is the torsional constant divided by the moment of inertia. From this, the time period for one full back-and-forth twist comes out to two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional constant. So a heavier or more spread-out object oscillates more slowly, and a stiffer wire makes it oscillate faster. This lets us actually measure the torsional constant of a wire just by timing the oscillations, which is exactly what the example will show us.

It depends only on how stiff the wire is, k, and how hard the disc is to spin, its moment of inertia I. <<POINT:disc>> <<PAUSE:short>> The time period is two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{k}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:twist-angle>> <<WRITE_KEY:T equals two pi root I over k|id=key-2>>The time period is two pi times the square root of I over k. A heavier disc swings slower; a stiffer wire swings faster. Notice the angle of twist is nowhere in there, so the period stays the same whether you twist it a little or a lot. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
Imagine a particle that feels not just one springy restoring force, but two at the same time. Each force on its own would make the particle do simple harmonic motion. So what happens when both act together? The beautiful answer comes straight from Newton's second law. If you write the equation for the first force alone, you get one motion. Write it for the second force alone, you get another. Now add those two equations together, and you discover something elegant: the actual position of the particle when both forces act is simply the vector sum of where each force would have placed it separately. So you can solve each motion independently and just add the positions. The same goes for velocities. This is called the principle of superposition, and it's a powerful shortcut.

Now let's look at two cases. First, when both simple harmonic motions are along the same direction, say both along the x-axis, with the same frequency but possibly different amplitudes and a phase difference. When you add them using trigonometry, the result is itself a simple harmonic motion of the same frequency. Its amplitude depends on the two individual amplitudes and the phase difference between them. If the two motions are perfectly in phase, the amplitudes simply add, giving the largest possible result. If they are exactly out of phase, they subtract, and if the amplitudes are equal, they cancel completely and the particle doesn't move at all. There's also a neat trick: you can represent each motion as a vector, draw the second at an angle equal to the phase difference, and the resultant vector gives you the resultant motion directly.

The second case is when the two motions are along perpendicular directions, one along x and one along y, again with the same frequency. Now the particle moves in two dimensions, and its path is generally an ellipse traced inside a rectangle whose sides are set by the two amplitudes. When the phase difference is zero, the ellipse collapses into a straight diagonal line. When the phase difference is pi, it becomes the other diagonal. When the phase difference is exactly ninety degrees, you get a proper upright ellipse, and if the two amplitudes are also equal, that ellipse becomes a perfect circle. So just by changing how out of step the two motions are, you can produce lines, ellipses, and circles. Notice how much richness comes from simply combining two simple back-and-forth motions.

What on earth does it actually do? <<POINT:origin>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:origin>> Here's the trap your brain falls into: you imagine the two motions fighting, tangling up into some hopeless mess that you'd need new physics to describe. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:origin>> But the answer is astonishingly simple, and it falls right out of Newton's second law. Let's just play fair and ask one force at a time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:vector_a>> <<SECTION:One force at a time|id=sec-1>>Pretend only the first force acts. By itself it gives the particle some position; call that position r one. <<TRACE:vector_a>> <<FOCUS:vector_b>> Now pretend instead that only the second force acts. By itself it would put the particle at a different position; call that r two. <<TRACE:vector_b>> Newton's second law for each force on its own says mass times the acceleration of that position equals that single force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2 r_1}{dt^2} = F_1, \qquad m\frac{d^2 r_2}{dt^2} = F_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:origin>> So if I solve each motion on its own, where does the particle really go when both forces act together at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant>> <<WRITE_KEY:Actual position r equals r1 plus r2, as vectors|id=key-1>>Watch. The real position is simply r one plus r two, tip to tail, the vector sum. Nothing fights, nothing tangles. <<TRACE:resultant>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant>> Why is nature this kind to us? Because Newton's second law adds. The mass times acceleration from the first equation, plus the same from the second, must equal the total force. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resultant>> And when you add those two equations, the left side becomes the acceleration of r one plus r two, while the right side becomes the resultant force. So that sum r one plus r two is exactly the true motion. <<PAUSE:short>> Adding the two equations, the mass times the acceleration of the sum r one plus r two equals the total of both forces, which is the real resultant force. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{d^2}{dt^2}(r_1 + r_2) = F_1 + F_2|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Velocities add too: u equals u1 plus u2|id=text-1>>The very same trick works for velocities. The real velocity is the velocity from force one plus the velocity from force two, added as vectors. <<POINT:resultant>> So the actual position is the vector sum of the two separate positions, and the actual velocity is the vector sum of the two separate velocities. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{r} = \vec{r_1} + \vec{r_2}, \qquad \vec{u} = \vec{u_1} + \vec{u_2}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have two simple harmonic motions along the x-axis with the same frequency. The first has an amplitude of two point zero centimeters, and the second also has an amplitude of two point zero centimeters. The phase difference between them is pi over three, which is sixty degrees. We want the amplitude of the combined motion. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Combine x1 = (2.0 cm) sin wt and x2 = (2.0 cm) sin(wt + pi/3); find resultant amplitude|id=ex-q-1>> Since both motions are along the same direction, we combine their amplitudes using the resultant amplitude formula: A equals the square root of A one squared plus A two squared plus two times A one times A two times cosine of delta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2 A_1 A_2 \cos\delta}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now we substitute the values. A one is two point zero centimeters, A two is two point zero centimeters, and delta is pi over three. <<WRITE_STEP:A = sqrt[(2.0 cm)^2 + (2.0 cm)^2 + 2(2.0 cm)^2 cos(pi/3)]|id=ex-step-1-1>> The cosine of pi over three equals one half, so the last term becomes two times two point zero squared times one half. <<WRITE_STEP:A = sqrt[4.0 + 4.0 + 2(4.0)(1/2)] cm = sqrt[12.0] cm|indent=1|id=ex-step-1-2>> Taking the square root, the resultant amplitude comes out to three point five centimeters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A = 3.5 cm|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:resultant>> This shortcut has a famous name, the principle of superposition. Solve each simple harmonic motion in peace, then just add the answers. <<TRACE:resultant>> <<FOCUS:resultant>> So two forces at once never need new physics. The actual position is the vector sum of where each force alone would have placed it, and that is the whole secret. <<PAUSE:short>>

12.12 DAMPED HARMONIC MOTION
A particle will execute a simple harmonic motion
with a constant amplitude if the resultant force on it
is proportional to the displacement and is directed
opposite to it. Nature provides a large number of
situations in which such restoring force acts. The
spring-mass system and the simple pendulum are
examples. However, in many of the cases some kind
of damping force is also present with the restoring
force. The damping force may arise due to friction
between the moving parts, air resistance or several
other causes. The damping force is a function of speed
of the moving system and is directed opposite to the
velocity. Energy is lost due to the negative work done
by the damping force and the system comes to a halt
in due course.

topics.our_understanding:
So far in this chapter, we've talked about a particle that swings or bounces back and forth forever, keeping the same size of swing every time. That happens when the only force pulling it back is a restoring force, one that's proportional to how far it's displaced and points back toward the center. The spring-mass system and the simple pendulum both work that way. But here's the honest truth about the real world: a swing never keeps swinging forever, and a vibrating spring eventually goes still. Why? Because there's almost always another force in the picture, and we call it a damping force.

Think about what slows things down. Friction between moving parts, air pushing against the motion, and other resistances. All of these act like a brake. The key thing about a damping force is that it depends on the speed of the moving object, and it always points opposite to the velocity. So whichever way the object is heading, the damping force pushes back against it. Because of that, the damping force does negative work, which means it constantly drains energy out of the system. Little by little the swings get weaker, and eventually the system comes to a halt.

Now, the damping force can be a complicated thing, but in many useful cases it's simply proportional to the speed. We write that the damping force equals some constant b times the velocity, directed against the motion. When you put that into the equation of motion alongside the restoring force, you get an equation that calculus can solve. For light damping, the solution looks like a sine wave whose amplitude shrinks over time. The amplitude at any moment equals the starting amplitude multiplied by an exponential decay factor that gets smaller as time passes.

Notice something nice here. When the damping is small, the angular frequency of the wobbling is almost exactly the natural frequency, the square root of k over m, the same frequency the system would have with no damping at all. So the rhythm barely changes, but the size of the swings keeps fading until it reaches zero. The diagram in the book shows this beautifully, a wave squeezed inside a shrinking envelope.

Finally, if the damping is really strong, the system may not oscillate at all. Displace it, and it just creeps back to the middle and stays there without ever overshooting to the other side. The exact amount of damping where oscillation just barely stops happening is called critical damping. That's an important idea in real devices, like the shock absorbers in a car.

topics.standalone_narration_text: Push a child on a swing once, then walk away. It swings high, then lower, then lower still, and a minute later it just hangs there, perfectly still. Up to now we pretended a swing keeps the same size forever, swinging back and forth with a steady amplitude, driven only by a restoring force pulling it toward the center. <<SECTION:The damping force|id=sec-1>>But the real world has a second force, a brake, and we call it the damping force. Friction, air resistance, anything that resists motion. Here is its defining habit: the damping force always points opposite to the velocity. Whichever way the object moves, this force pushes back against it. <<PAUSE:short>> The braking force points opposite to the velocity, and for many real cases its size is just proportional to how fast the thing is moving. <<WRITE_EQUATION:F_{\text{damp}} = -bv|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_TEXT:damping force opposes velocity|id=text-1>>And in many real situations its strength is simply proportional to the speed, so we write the damping force as minus b times v. Now, a force that always opposes the velocity does negative work on the object every single moment of the motion. Negative work means it steadily removes energy. <<PAUSE:short>> So here is the honest question: if energy keeps leaking out swing after swing, what happens to the size of the swing over time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:oscillation-curve>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_12:damped_oscillation_curve>> Each swing carries a little less energy than the last, so each swing reaches a little less far. The amplitude shrinks, swing after swing, until the motion dies. <<TRACE:oscillation-curve>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:envelope-upper>> <<SECTION:The decaying envelope|id=sec-2>>Watch the peaks. They sit inside two smooth curves that close in toward the center line, an envelope that squeezes the motion down to nothing. <<TRACE:envelope-upper>> The motion is still a sine wave, but its amplitude is no longer fixed; it's multiplied by a shrinking exponential that fades the swing away. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = A_0\, e^{-\frac{bt}{2m}} \sin(\omega t + \phi)|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:amplitude decays inside a shrinking exponential envelope|id=key-1>>The first swing is the tallest, and from there every peak hides beneath a fading exponential curve, all the way down to rest. <<TRACE:envelope-lower>> <<POINT:envelope-lower>> But notice the rhythm between the peaks barely changes. For light damping the system still oscillates with almost its natural frequency, the same frequency it would have with no brake at all. <<POINT:first-peak>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rest-point>> So a damped oscillation is two ideas in one picture: the familiar back-and-forth rhythm, riding inside an amplitude that quietly fades to zero, right here at the resting point.

12.13 FORCED OSCILLATION AND RESONANCE
In certain situations apart from the restoring force
and the damping force, there is yet another force
applied on the body which itself changes periodically

If the damping were ideally zero, the amplitude of
the forced vibration at resonance would be infinity by
equation (12.31). Some damping is always present in
mechanical systems and the amplitude remains finite.
However, the amplitude may become very large if
the damping is small and the applied frequency is close
to the natural frequency. This effect is important in
designing bridges and other civil constructions. On
July 1, 1940, the newly constructed Tacoma Narrows
Bridge (Washington) was opened for traffic. Only four
months after this, a mild wind set up the bridge in
resonant vibrations. In a few hours the amplitude
became so large that the bridge could not stand the
stress and a part broke off and went into the water
below.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens when you keep pushing on something that already likes to oscillate. Up to now we've imagined a body with a restoring force pulling it back toward the center, plus a damping force that slowly drains its energy away. Left alone, such a body would eventually stop. But now imagine you add a third force, an outside push that itself rises and falls in a regular, repeating way over time. We call this a driving force, and the motion it creates is called forced oscillation.

Here's the interesting part. At first the motion looks messy and complicated, but after a little while the body settles down and starts oscillating at the same frequency as the force you're applying, not at its own natural frequency. The outside push is now in charge of the rhythm. And because the driving force keeps feeding in energy to replace whatever the damping steals away, the oscillation keeps going forever with a steady, constant size. That's the key idea: the energy lost to damping is exactly compensated by the work done by the applied force, so the swinging is sustained.

Now think about the size of that steady swing, its amplitude. It depends on how close the frequency of your push is to the body's own natural frequency. When you tune the driving frequency to match, the amplitude shoots up dramatically. This special condition is called resonance. If the damping is small, the natural frequency and the resonance frequency are almost the same, and the response is sharp. Sharp means the amplitude is huge right at resonance but falls off quickly if you move even a little away from it.

Notice something striking. If there were no damping at all, the formula says the amplitude at resonance would become infinite. In real life there's always some damping, so the amplitude stays finite, but it can still grow enormously when damping is small and your driving frequency sits close to the natural one.

This isn't just abstract. Engineers worry about it. A famous and tragic example is the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington. It opened in nineteen forty, and only four months later a mild wind set it into resonant vibrations. Over a few hours the amplitude grew so large that the bridge tore itself apart and collapsed into the water below. That's resonance in action, and it's why builders take it so seriously.

events.text: Free swing decays to rest
Driven body oscillates at the driving frequency, not its natural one
Resonance: drive at the natural frequency and amplitude can become huge

topics.standalone_narration_text: Soldiers marching in perfect step are ordered to break stride before crossing a bridge. Why would an army be afraid of walking in time? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer is hiding in a single idea: what happens when you keep pushing on something that already likes to swing back and forth. Think of a child on a swing. Left alone after one push, friction and air slowly drain the energy and the swing dies down. <<WRITE_TEXT:Free swing decays to rest|id=text-1>> But now you stand behind and give a gentle push, again and again, on your own rhythm. That repeating outside push is what we call a driving force, and the motion it creates is forced oscillation. <<SECTION:Forced oscillation|id=sec-1>> Here is the surprising part. The swing has its own favourite rhythm, its natural frequency. But push it at a different rhythm, and after a messy moment it gives in and swings at your rhythm, not its own. <<PAUSE:short>> The driver takes charge of the beat. The body ends up oscillating at the frequency of the force you apply. <<WRITE_KEY:Driven body oscillates at the driving frequency, not its natural one|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> And because every push tops up the energy that damping steals away, the swinging no longer dies out. It settles to a steady, constant size. The body feels three things at once: the spring pulling it back, the damping dragging it down, and the outside push that rises and falls with time. <<WRITE_EQUATION:m\frac{dv}{dt} = -kx - bv + F_0\sin(\omega t)|id=eq-1|boxed>> So here is the real question: if I can push at any rhythm I like, does it matter which one I choose? Is every rhythm just as good? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:curve-heavy-damping>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:simple_harmonic_motion:12_13:resonance_curve>> Watch what happens to the size of the swing as I change my pushing frequency. Here is the amplitude plotted against the driving frequency. <<TRACE:curve-heavy-damping>> When my pushing rhythm matches the swing's own natural rhythm, the amplitude shoots up to a peak. Pushing in time with its favourite beat pours energy in most efficiently. <<SECTION:Resonance|id=sec-2>> <<POINT:natural-freq-line>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:resonance-peak>> This matching condition has a name: resonance. And now look at what damping does to the picture. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:curve-light-damping>> With heavy damping the peak is low and broad. But with light damping the peak becomes a towering, razor-sharp spike, the amplitude growing enormous near the natural frequency. <<TRACE:curve-light-damping>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> We can put numbers on it. The steady amplitude depends on how far your driving frequency sits from the natural frequency, and on the damping. The steady amplitude is large when the driving frequency omega sits close to the natural frequency omega-naught, and it is held in check by the damping term underneath. <<WRITE_EQUATION:A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> Now the soldiers make sense. March in step at just the wrong rhythm and you become a driving force on the bridge. Hit its natural frequency, with little damping to save you, and the resonant swing can grow until the bridge tears itself apart. <<WRITE_KEY:Resonance: drive at the natural frequency and amplitude can become huge|id=key-2>>
