questions.q_text: In simple harmonic motion, when the particle is displaced to the positive side of the centre, in which direction does its acceleration point?
options: A. Toward the centre, in the negative direction
B. Away from the centre, in the positive direction
C. It has no acceleration at that point
D. Perpendicular to the line of motion

questions.q_text: What is true about the force acting on a particle in SHM when it is exactly at the centre of oscillation?
options: A. The force is at its maximum value
B. The force is zero because displacement is zero
C. The force points away from the centre
D. The force equals mass times omega squared

questions.q_text: Which of the following best captures what makes an oscillation a simple harmonic motion rather than just any back-and-forth motion?
options: A. The motion repeats after equal intervals of time
B. The particle moves along a curved path
C. The restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed toward a fixed point
D. The speed of the particle stays constant throughout

questions.q_text: A particle of mass 2 kilograms moves in simple harmonic motion with omega equal to 5 radians per second. Find the force constant k, and then find the force on the particle when it is 0.1 metres from the centre.
questions.answer: Step 1: The force constant is defined as k equals mass times omega squared. So k equals 2 times (5 squared) equals 2 times 25 equals 50. Thus k equals 50 newtons per metre. Step 2: The force in SHM is force equals negative k times x. With x equal to 0.1 metres, force equals negative 50 times 0.1 equals negative 5 newtons. Step 3: The magnitude of the force is 5 newtons, and the negative sign tells us it is directed back toward the centre (the equilibrium position).

questions.q_text: A particle in simple harmonic motion has omega equal to 4 radians per second. At a certain instant it is 0.2 metres to the negative side of the centre, meaning x equals negative 0.2 metres. Find its acceleration at that instant and state its direction.
questions.answer: Step 1: The defining equation of SHM is acceleration equals negative omega squared times x. Step 2: Omega squared equals 4 squared equals 16. Step 3: Substitute x equals negative 0.2: acceleration equals negative 16 times (negative 0.2) equals positive 3.2 metres per second squared. Step 4: The acceleration is positive 3.2 metres per second squared, which is directed toward the centre. This makes sense because the particle is on the negative side, so it must be pushed back in the positive direction toward equilibrium.

questions.q_text: As the block in the spring system moves through simple harmonic motion, in which direction does the spring force always point?
options: A. In the direction of the block's motion
B. Always toward the center point O
C. Always away from the center point O
D. In a constant direction regardless of displacement

questions.q_text: At which point during the motion does the block have its maximum speed?
options: A. At point P, the release point
B. At point Q, the far side
C. At the center O
D. Halfway between O and P

questions.q_text: At the extreme points P and Q, how is the total mechanical energy distributed?
options: A. Entirely kinetic energy
B. Entirely potential energy stored in the spring
C. Split equally between kinetic and potential
D. Zero, because the block is at rest

questions.q_text: What is the fundamental reason the distance OP equals the distance OQ in this frictionless system?
options: A. The spring constant is the same on both sides
B. Energy conservation requires equal potential energy at both turning points
C. The block always moves at constant speed
D. The minus sign in the force law cancels out

questions.q_text: Suppose the table were NOT frictionless and a small amount of friction acted on the block. Qualitatively, how would the motion change, and would the distances OP and OQ still be equal? Explain using the energy ideas from this section.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall the energy picture. In the frictionless case, energy sloshes back and forth between spring potential energy (at the ends) and block kinetic energy (at the center), with the total staying constant. Because no energy is lost, the potential energy at P equals the potential energy at Q, which forces OP to equal OQ. Step 2: Add friction. Friction is a force that removes mechanical energy from the system, converting it into heat as the block slides. Step 3: Consequence over one swing. When the block travels from P to the other side, some energy is lost to friction along the way. So when it momentarily stops at Q, it has less total energy than it had at P. Less energy means less spring potential energy, which means the block stops closer to the center. Therefore OQ would be smaller than OP. Step 4: Long-term behavior. Each successive swing loses more energy, so the turning points get closer and closer to O. The amplitude steadily shrinks until the block eventually comes to rest at the center. Conclusion: With friction, OP and OQ are no longer equal (the second turning point is closer to O), and the motion is a decaying oscillation rather than a forever-repeating one.

questions.q_text: A block of mass 2 kilograms is attached to a spring of spring constant 200 newtons per meter on a frictionless table. As it passes through the center O, its speed is 4 meters per second. Using energy conservation, find the amplitude of the motion.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the energy at the center. At O the spring is at its natural length, so all the energy is kinetic. Kinetic energy equals one-half times mass times speed squared. That is one-half times 2 times (4 times 4) = one-half times 2 times 16 = 16 joules. Step 2: Identify the energy at the extreme. At the turning point (distance A from center), the block is momentarily at rest, so all the energy is spring potential energy, which equals one-half times k times A squared. Step 3: Set them equal by energy conservation. 16 = one-half times 200 times A squared, so 16 = 100 times A squared. Step 4: Solve for A. A squared = 16 divided by 100 = 0.16, so A = the square root of 0.16 = 0.4 meters. Conclusion: The amplitude of the motion is 0.4 meters.

questions.q_text: In the force law for simple harmonic motion, the force equals negative k times x. What is the physical significance of that minus sign?
options: A. It means the force always points back toward the center, restoring the particle
B. It means the particle has negative mass
C. It means the force increases without limit forever
D. It means the particle moves only in the negative direction

questions.q_text: According to the velocity equation derived in this section, where is the particle's speed equal to zero?
options: A. At the center, where x is zero
B. At the extreme positions, where x equals plus or minus the amplitude
C. Halfway between the center and the edge
D. The speed is never zero during the motion

questions.q_text: Position follows a sine curve in time and velocity follows a cosine curve. By how much are these two out of step?
options: A. Half a cycle
B. A full cycle
C. A quarter cycle
D. They are perfectly in step

questions.q_text: A particle of mass 0.5 kilograms undergoes simple harmonic motion with a force constant k equal to 8 newtons per meter. Find the angular frequency omega of the motion.
questions.answer: Omega squared is defined as k divided by m. Here k is 8 newtons per meter and m is 0.5 kilograms. So omega squared equals 8 divided by 0.5, which is 16. Taking the square root, omega equals 4 radians per second. So the angular frequency of the oscillation is 4 radians per second.

questions.q_text: A particle in simple harmonic motion has amplitude 0.1 meters and angular frequency 5 radians per second. Find the maximum speed of the particle, and explain where in the motion this maximum occurs.
questions.answer: The velocity equation is velocity equals omega times the square root of A squared minus x squared. The speed is largest when the quantity under the square root is largest, which happens when x equals zero, that is, at the center. There the speed equals omega times A. Substituting, maximum speed equals 5 times 0.1, which is 0.5 meters per second. This maximum occurs as the particle passes through the center of its motion, where it moves fastest, consistent with the cosine velocity curve reaching its peak when the sine position is zero.

questions.q_text: A particle oscillates with amplitude 5 centimeters and angular frequency 2 radians per second. What is its speed when it is 3 centimeters from the center?
questions.answer: Use velocity equals omega times the square root of A squared minus x squared. Here A is 5 centimeters and x is 3 centimeters. A squared is 25 and x squared is 9, so A squared minus x squared is 16. The square root of 16 is 4 centimeters. Multiply by omega, which is 2 per second: velocity equals 2 times 4, which is 8 centimeters per second. So the particle's speed at that point is 8 centimeters per second.

questions.q_text: If you replace the block on a spring with a heavier one while keeping the same spring, what happens to the time period of the oscillation?
options: A. It increases
B. It decreases
C. It stays exactly the same
D. It becomes zero

questions.q_text: At an instant when the phase of a particle in simple harmonic motion equals zero, where is the particle and what is it doing?
options: A. At the positive extreme, momentarily at rest
B. At the negative extreme, momentarily at rest
C. Crossing the mean position moving in the positive direction
D. Crossing the mean position moving in the negative direction

questions.q_text: Why are the sine form and cosine form of simple harmonic motion considered the same motion?
options: A. Because they have different amplitudes
B. Because they differ only in the phase constant, set by when you start the stopwatch
C. Because cosine motion is twice as fast as sine motion
D. Because only cosine motion has a defined time period

questions.q_text: If the time period of an oscillation is one quarter of a second, what is its frequency?
options: A. 0.25 hertz
B. 1 hertz
C. 4 hertz
D. 16 hertz

questions.q_text: A block of mass 2 kilograms is attached to a spring with force constant 8 newtons per metre. Find the angular frequency, the time period, and the frequency of the resulting simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Angular frequency. Omega equals the square root of k divided by m. Here k is 8 and m is 2, so k over m equals 4. The square root of 4 is 2. So omega equals 2 radians per second.

Step 2: Time period. T equals two pi divided by omega. That is two pi divided by 2, which equals pi seconds, approximately 3.14 seconds.

Step 3: Frequency. Frequency equals one divided by the time period. That is one divided by pi, approximately 0.318 hertz.

So the angular frequency is 2 radians per second, the time period is about 3.14 seconds, and the frequency is about 0.32 hertz.

questions.q_text: A particle in simple harmonic motion has displacement that swings between minus 5 centimetres and plus 5 centimetres from the center. What is its amplitude?
options: A. 10 centimetres
B. 5 centimetres
C. 2.5 centimetres
D. 0 centimetres

questions.q_text: A particle moves uniformly around a circle of radius A, starting on the X-axis. What is the position of its shadow on the X-axis at time t?
options: A. A times the sine of omega t
B. A times the cosine of omega t
C. A times omega times t
D. A divided by the cosine of omega t

questions.q_text: The shadows of the circling particle on the X-axis and Y-axis both perform simple harmonic motion. By how much do their phases differ?
options: A. Zero
B. pi over four radians
C. pi over two radians
D. pi radians

questions.q_text: According to the projection idea, what kind of motion do you get when you project uniform circular motion onto any diameter of the circle?
options: A. Uniform straight-line motion
B. Simple harmonic motion
C. Accelerated motion with increasing speed
D. Random oscillation

questions.q_text: For the shadow performing simple harmonic motion, how do its amplitude and angular frequency relate to the circular motion?
options: A. Amplitude equals the radius A and angular frequency equals omega
B. Amplitude equals twice the radius and frequency equals half of omega
C. Amplitude equals omega and frequency equals A
D. Both amplitude and frequency depend on time t

questions.q_text: A particle moves around a circle of radius 5 centimetres with angular speed 2 radians per second, starting on the X-axis at time zero. Find the position of its shadow on the X-axis at time equal to one quarter of pi seconds.
questions.answer: The shadow on the X-axis follows simple harmonic motion given by position equals A times the cosine of omega t. Here A is 5 centimetres and omega is 2 radians per second. At time t equal to pi over four seconds, omega times t equals 2 times pi over four, which is pi over two radians. The cosine of pi over two is zero. So the position is 5 times zero, which equals zero. The shadow is exactly at the centre (origin) at that moment.

questions.q_text: Explain why the shadow on the Y-axis also performs simple harmonic motion, and why it follows a sine while the X-axis shadow follows a cosine.
questions.answer: As the particle circles steadily, the line from the centre to the particle makes angle omega t with the X-axis. Dropping a perpendicular to the Y-axis gives a shadow whose position is A times the sine of omega t. Since this is of the form (amplitude) times (sine of angular frequency times time), it is exactly the equation of simple harmonic motion, with the same amplitude A and the same angular frequency omega as the X-axis shadow. The difference is that the X-axis shadow projects horizontally giving A cosine of omega t, while the Y-axis shadow projects vertically giving A sine of omega t. Because cosine of omega t equals sine of omega t plus pi over two, the two motions are identical in form but shifted in phase by a quarter turn, that is by pi over two radians.

questions.q_text: For a block oscillating on a spring, what is true about the energy when the block passes through the center of its motion?
options: A. All the energy is potential and kinetic energy is zero
B. All the energy is kinetic and potential energy is zero
C. Energy is split equally between kinetic and potential
D. Both kinetic and potential energy are at their maximum

questions.q_text: When we add the kinetic and potential energies in simple harmonic motion, why does the total turn out to be constant in time?
options: A. Because the force is always zero
B. Because sine squared plus cosine squared always equals one, removing the time dependence
C. Because the amplitude slowly decreases
D. Because potential energy is always zero

questions.q_text: At the extreme ends of the motion, where displacement equals plus or minus the amplitude, what is the value of the potential energy?
options: A. Zero
B. One half k times A squared
C. One quarter k times A squared
D. It cannot be determined

questions.q_text: A block of mass 2 kilograms oscillates on a spring with force constant 200 newtons per meter and amplitude 0.1 meters. Find the total energy of the system, and then find the kinetic energy when the block is at a displacement of 0.06 meters from the center.
questions.answer: Step 1: Total energy equals one half k times A squared. So total energy = 0.5 times 200 times (0.1 squared) = 0.5 times 200 times 0.01 = 1 joule. Step 2: Potential energy at x = 0.06 m is one half k times x squared = 0.5 times 200 times (0.06 squared) = 0.5 times 200 times 0.0036 = 0.36 joules. Step 3: Since total energy is conserved, kinetic energy = total energy minus potential energy = 1 minus 0.36 = 0.64 joules. So the kinetic energy at that point is 0.64 joules.

questions.q_text: A 0.5 kilogram block on a spring has total energy 1 joule. What is its maximum speed, which occurs at the center of the motion?
questions.answer: Step 1: At the center, all the energy is kinetic, so kinetic energy equals the total energy = 1 joule. Step 2: Kinetic energy = one half times mass times speed squared. So 1 = 0.5 times 0.5 times v squared = 0.25 times v squared. Step 3: Solve for v squared: v squared = 1 divided by 0.25 = 4. Step 4: Take the square root: v = 2 meters per second. So the maximum speed is 2 meters per second.

questions.q_text: For a twisting oscillation to count as angular simple harmonic motion, what must be true about the torque when the body is turned away from its rest position?
options: A. The torque must be constant no matter how far the body is turned
B. The torque must be proportional to the angle and point back toward the rest position
C. The torque must increase the angle even further away from rest
D. The torque must be zero at every angle

questions.q_text: If you replace a swinging body with a heavier, more spread-out one while keeping the restoring torque constant, what happens to the time period of its angular oscillation?
options: A. The period gets shorter, so it swings faster
B. The period gets longer, so it swings slower
C. The period stays exactly the same
D. The body stops oscillating entirely

questions.q_text: As the body swings through angular simple harmonic motion, which statement about its energy is correct?
options: A. The total energy slowly decreases as the body swings
B. Potential and kinetic energy both reach maximum at the same instant
C. Energy trades between potential and kinetic, but the total stays constant
D. The kinetic energy is largest at the maximum angle

questions.q_text: A body undergoes angular simple harmonic motion. Its moment of inertia is 2 kilogram metre squared, and the restoring torque constant k is 8 newton metre per radian. Find the angular frequency and the time period of the oscillation.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall that the angular frequency omega is the square root of k divided by I. Here k equals 8 and I equals 2. So omega equals the square root of 8 divided by 2, which is the square root of 4, which equals 2 radians per second. Step 2: The time period is two pi times the square root of I divided by k, which is also two pi divided by omega. So the period equals two pi divided by 2, which equals pi seconds, approximately 3.14 seconds. So the angular frequency is 2 radians per second and the period is about 3.14 seconds.

questions.q_text: A torsional oscillator has a certain time period. If the restoring torque constant k is increased to four times its original value while the moment of inertia stays the same, what happens to the time period?
options: A. It becomes four times longer
B. It is cut in half
C. It becomes four times shorter (one quarter)
D. It is unchanged

questions.q_text: According to the simple pendulum formula, which of these quantities affects the time period of a swing?
options: A. The mass of the ball
B. The length of the string
C. The amplitude of the swing (for large swings only)
D. The material the ball is made of

questions.q_text: Why does a simple pendulum behave as a simple harmonic oscillator only for small swings?
options: A. Because at small angles the tension becomes zero
B. Because at small angles the sine of the angle is nearly equal to the angle itself, making the torque proportional to the angle
C. Because at large angles the mass changes
D. Because gravity only acts during small swings

questions.q_text: Why does the tension in the string create no torque about the swinging axis?
options: A. Because tension is always smaller than the weight
B. Because tension points along the string straight toward the pivot, so it has no lever arm about the pivot
C. Because tension acts only at the equilibrium position
D. Because tension is perpendicular to the string

questions.q_text: A simple pendulum has a string of length 1 meter. Taking gravity as about 10 meters per second squared, find its time period for small swings.
questions.answer: The period equals two pi times the square root of the length divided by gravity. Step 1: Divide length by gravity: 1 divided by 10 equals 0.1. Step 2: Take the square root of 0.1, which is about 0.316. Step 3: Multiply by two pi (about 6.283): 6.283 times 0.316 is about 1.99. So the time period is approximately 2 seconds.

questions.q_text: In a lab, a pendulum of length 0.25 meters is found to have a time period of 1 second. Use this to estimate the value of gravity.
questions.answer: Start with period equals two pi times the square root of length over gravity. Square both sides: period squared equals four pi squared times length over gravity. Rearrange for gravity: gravity equals four pi squared times length divided by period squared. Plug in: four pi squared is about 39.48. Multiply by length 0.25: 39.48 times 0.25 equals 9.87. Divide by period squared (1 squared is 1): gravity is about 9.87 meters per second squared. This matches the standard value of g.

questions.q_text: If you make the string of a pendulum four times longer, what happens to its time period?
options: A. It doubles
B. It becomes four times larger
C. It is cut in half
D. It stays the same

questions.q_text: In a physical pendulum hanging from point O, which force is responsible for producing the restoring torque that brings it back to rest?
options: A. The support force acting at O
B. The weight acting at the centre of mass
C. Air resistance on the body
D. The normal force from the axis

questions.q_text: Why is the motion of a physical pendulum not truly simple harmonic motion in general?
options: A. Because the angular acceleration is proportional to the angle itself
B. Because there is no restoring torque at all
C. Because the angular acceleration is proportional to the sine of the angle, not the angle
D. Because the moment of inertia changes as it swings

questions.q_text: What approximation allows us to treat a physical pendulum's small swings as simple harmonic motion?
options: A. Replacing mass with weight
B. Taking the sine of a small angle as approximately equal to the angle in radians
C. Ignoring the moment of inertia
D. Assuming gravity is zero

questions.q_text: According to the time period formula for a physical pendulum, increasing the moment of inertia while keeping everything else fixed will do what to the period?
options: A. Decrease the period
B. Increase the period
C. Leave the period unchanged
D. Make the motion stop

questions.q_text: A uniform rod of mass 0.5 kilograms and length 1.2 metres is pivoted at one end and allowed to swing as a physical pendulum. The moment of inertia of a rod about one end is one third times mass times length squared, and its centre of mass is at the midpoint. Taking gravity as 10 metres per second squared, find the time period of small oscillations.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Find the moment of inertia about the pivot end. I = (1/3) times mass times length squared = (1/3)(0.5)(1.2 squared) = (1/3)(0.5)(1.44) = (1/3)(0.72) = 0.24 kilogram metre squared.

Step 2: Find the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass. For a uniform rod pivoted at one end, the centre of mass is at the midpoint, so distance = 1.2 / 2 = 0.6 metres.

Step 3: Use the time period formula: T = 2 pi times square root of ( I divided by (mass times gravity times distance) ).

Denominator = mass times gravity times distance = 0.5 times 10 times 0.6 = 3.

So the ratio = 0.24 / 3 = 0.08.

Square root of 0.08 = 0.2828 approximately.

Step 4: T = 2 pi times 0.2828 = 6.283 times 0.2828 = 1.777 seconds.

So the time period is about 1.78 seconds.

questions.q_text: In a physical pendulum, the resting position (zero angle) corresponds to which configuration?
options: A. The centre of mass directly above the pivot
B. The centre of mass hanging straight down below the pivot
C. The centre of mass level with the pivot horizontally
D. The body lying flat on a surface

questions.q_text: In a torsional pendulum, what does the restoring torque depend on?
options: A. It is constant regardless of how much the disc is twisted
B. It is proportional to the angle through which the disc is twisted
C. It is proportional to the square of the angle of twist
D. It depends only on the moment of inertia of the disc

questions.q_text: If you replace the disc on a torsional pendulum with a heavier, more spread-out disc while keeping the same wire, what happens to the time period of oscillation?
options: A. It increases
B. It decreases
C. It stays exactly the same
D. It becomes zero

questions.q_text: Which quantity in a torsional pendulum plays the same role that the spring constant plays in an ordinary spring-mass system?
options: A. The moment of inertia
B. The angle of twist
C. The torsional constant of the wire
D. The length of the wire

questions.q_text: Two identical discs are hung from two different wires. Wire 1 has a larger torsional constant than wire 2. Which disc oscillates faster?
options: A. The one on wire 1, because a stiffer wire gives a shorter period
B. The one on wire 2, because a softer wire gives a shorter period
C. Both oscillate at the same rate since the discs are identical
D. Neither will oscillate at all

questions.q_text: A disc with a moment of inertia of 0.02 kilogram metre squared is hung from a wire and twisted. It completes one full oscillation in 2 seconds. Find the torsional constant of the wire.
questions.answer: Start with the time period formula for a torsional pendulum: the period equals two pi times the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the torsional constant. Step 1: Write the relationship. T = 2 pi times sqrt(I / C), where I is the moment of inertia and C is the torsional constant. Step 2: Square both sides to remove the square root. T squared = 4 times pi squared times (I / C). Step 3: Solve for C. C = 4 times pi squared times I divided by T squared. Step 4: Substitute the values. I = 0.02, T = 2 so T squared = 4. C = (4 times 9.87 times 0.02) / 4. Step 5: Compute. 4 times pi squared is about 39.48. Multiply by 0.02 to get about 0.7896. Divide by 4 to get about 0.197. So the torsional constant is approximately 0.197 newton metre per radian.

questions.q_text: A particle is acted on by two simple harmonic motions along the same line, both of the same frequency and both of amplitude 6 centimetres, but they are exactly out of phase (phase difference of pi). Describe the resultant motion and explain why.
questions.answer: Step 1: When two same-direction simple harmonic motions of the same frequency combine, the result is a simple harmonic motion of the same frequency whose amplitude depends on the two amplitudes and the phase difference between them. Step 2: When the phase difference is pi, the two motions are exactly out of phase, so they subtract rather than add. Step 3: The resultant amplitude is the difference of the two amplitudes: 6 centimetres minus 6 centimetres equals 0. Step 4: Since the amplitudes are equal and exactly out of phase, they cancel completely. The resultant amplitude is zero, so the particle does not move at all — at every instant one motion pushes it exactly as far as the other pulls it back.

questions.q_text: Explain what 'critical damping' means and why it matters in something like a car's shock absorbers.
questions.answer: Critical damping is the exact amount of damping at which the system just barely stops oscillating. With less damping than this (light damping), the object swings back and forth while the swings shrink. With critical damping, if you displace the object it simply creeps back to the center and stays there without ever overshooting to the other side. This is important for shock absorbers because you want the car to return smoothly to its resting level after hitting a bump. If damping were too weak, the car would bounce up and down repeatedly (uncomfortable and unsafe); if it were too strong, it would respond sluggishly. Critical damping (or close to it) gives the fastest return to equilibrium without oscillating, providing a smooth, controlled ride.

questions.q_text: Two identical pendulums are driven at resonance, but one has very small damping and the other has large damping. Explain how their responses differ, both right at resonance and slightly away from it.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall that resonance amplitude depends on damping. When damping is small, the amplitude at resonance becomes very large because little energy is being drained, so the energy fed in by the driving force builds up the swing enormously. Step 2: The pendulum with large damping has a much smaller peak amplitude at resonance, because more energy is being removed each cycle, limiting how big the swing can grow. Step 3: Now consider moving the driving frequency slightly away from resonance. For the small-damping pendulum, the response is sharp — the amplitude is huge exactly at resonance but falls off quickly as you move even a little away. Step 4: For the large-damping pendulum, the response is broad and flat — the amplitude is smaller overall but changes only gradually as the driving frequency moves away. Conclusion: Small damping gives a tall, sharp resonance peak; large damping gives a low, broad one.
